Crop Nutrient Balance
description: The Crop Nutrient Balance data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use (UMN IonE) and the Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC). This map shows the excess or deficit of elemental nitrogen and phosphorus globally at a 5 arc minute resolution. These data represent the year 2000 but were calculated from input data sets ranging from 1994-2001. The addition of these nutrients to croplands has led to widespread increases in agricultural productivity; however, this act has also increased nutrient pollution, especially in bodies of water. Converting atmospheric nitrogen and mining phosphorus also incur energy costs. The excess or deficit of nutrients is calculated using a simple mass balance. Inputs for nitrogen include chemical fertilizer, manure, nitrogen deposition and nitrogen fixation by legumes, which is scaled by yields. Phosphorus inputs include chemical fertilizer and manure. Nutrient removal from harvest is calculated as the product of yield, dry fraction and nutrient density. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Greenhouse Gas Emissions by Country and Economic Sector
description: ### Overview This dataset contains internationally comparable emissions data on greenhouse gasses (GHG) from 1990 to 2018. Additionally, it further shows GHG emissions for six individual economic sectors and subsectors on a global scale. The GHGs include carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆), and nitrous oxide (N₂O). The economic sectors included in the Resource Watch map are agriculture, bunker fuels, energy, industrial processes, and land-use change/forestry, and waste. This dataset is released by the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the larger Climate Analysis Indicators Tools (CAIT) Climate Data Explorer. This dataset is essential to help inform policymakers, researchers, and other stakeholders on countries’ climate progress. This dataset is featured in Facebook’s newly launched [Climate Science Center](https://www.facebook.com/climatescienceinfo/). The Resource Watch team provided data processing for Facebook with the goal of demonstrating historical GHG emissions from 1990 through 2018, and Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) for select countries. Learn more about our data processing on our [GitHub](https://github.com/resource-watch/blog-analysis/tree/master/req_020_facebook_ghg_emissions). ### Methodology Country GHG emissions data were collected from respected research centers, government agencies, and international bodies. To compile the country GHG emissions dataset WRI largely relied on data reported by countries to the United Nations Framework Convention (UNFCCC). To compliment this and create a broader picture of sector level GHG emissions estimates, WRI also consulted data from three nongovernmental sources: Carbon Dioxide Information Analysis Center (of the U.S. Dept. of Energy) (CDIAC), Energy Information Administration (of the U.S. Dept. of Energy) EIA, and the International Energy Agency (IEA). The data sources were selected based on criteria like accuracy and temporal and geographic coverage ranges. Country datasets were produced by employing a consistent methodology. Sector-level GHGemissions estimates were taken from the same sources as country level GHG emission data. Additionally, emissions data onLand Use Change and Forestry (LUCF) came from the Statistics Division of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). The final product has sector level GHG emissions data available for agriculture, industrial processes, energy, bunker fuels, land use and forestry, and waste. The datasets on bunker fuels includes data on carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions. Energy and land use/forestry further includes methane (CH₄)) and nitrogen dioxide (N₂O) in their dataset. The dataset on industrial processes includes data on the three GHGs described above and hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs). The dataset on agriculture only includes CH₄ and N₂O. The final dataset is presented in tabular format at a national scale. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://cait.wri.org/docs/CAIT2.0_CountryGHG_Methods.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for historical country-level CO₂ emissions data going back to 1850, and energy sub-sector CO₂ emissions data going back to 1971 are also available from the data provider. Energy subsector data is available for building, electrical/heat, fugitive emissions, manufacturing/construction, other fuel combustion, and transportation. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [GitHub](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_008_greenhouse_gas_emissions_country_sector). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Eutrophication and Hypoxia
description: The Interactive Map of Eutrophication & Hypoxia represents 762 coastal areas impacted by eutrophication and/or hypoxia. There are 479 sites identified as experiencing hypoxia, 55 sites that once experienced hypoxia but are now improving, and 228 sites that experience other symptoms of eutrophication, including algal blooms, species loss, and impacts to coral reef assemblages. These data were compiled using a literature search conducted by Dr. Robert Diaz of VIMS and WRI staff. Three types of status were recorded: 1) Hypoxic: Areas with scientiﬁc evidence that hypoxia was caused, at least in part, by nutrient overenrichment; 2) Eutrophic: Systems that exhibit effects of eutrophication, such as elevated nutrient levels, elevated chlorophyll a levels, harmful algal blooms, changes in the benthic community, damage to coral reefs, and ﬁsh kills. These systems are impaired by nutrients and are possibly at risk of developing hypoxia. Some of the systems classiﬁed as areas of concern may already be experiencing hypoxia, but lack conclusive scientiﬁc evidence of the condition; and 3) Improved hypoxic: Areas that once exhibited low dissolved oxygen levels and hypoxia, but are now improving. For example, the Black Sea once experienced annual hypoxic events, but is now in a state of recovery. Others, like Boston Harbor in the United States and the Mersey Estuary in the United Kingdom, also have improved water quality resulting from better industrial and wastewater controls. Average Temperature
description: Annual average temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps: All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value. All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value. Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2. The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Gridded Carbon Footprint
description: ### Overview The Gridded Carbon Footprint dataset shows a gridded estimate of absolute and per capita carbon emissions in the year 2013 for 189 countries. The results were produced by the Gridded Global Model of Carbon Footprints (GGMCF) model at a spatial resolution of 250 meters. GGMCF is based on previously available data for carbon footprint (CF), population, and household spending. The model uses urban vs. rural consumption patterns and purchasing power as the main indicators of per capita footprint. Higher purchasing power generally increases the chance of participating in activities that lead to more carbon emissions. The dataset was created by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) in collaboration with Shinshu University, Yale, and Lund University. Most cities, towns, and rural areas around the world have no carbon footprint data. This dataset provides the first internationally comparable CF estimates for many regions of the world. The results presented here can help develop strategies to reduce carbon footprint. Additionally, this dataset can be used by national governments to locate small regions with disproportionally high emissions rates. ### Methodology The dataset was created in four distinct steps: 1. National CFs of consumption (CFn) data were taken from the Eora multi-region input-output (MRIO) database for the year 2015. This data included 189 countries and accounted for close to 100% of global CO₂ emission. 2. For the EU, UK, USA, Japan, and China, existing subnational CF models were available from a variety of publications. These models were used to separate national CF of consumption data into subnational/regional data CFr. The size of regions ranged from ZIP codes to provinces. In steps 3 and 4 these subnational regions are treated the same as countries. Regions included the disaggregated subnational regions along with countries that are not disaggregated. 3. Within each region, the CFr was further disaggregated into urban and rural residents utilizing urban vs. rural population data and urban vs. rural expenditure pattern data from the World Bank, Eurostat, and US BEA. This data included 113 countries and accounted for 81% of global CO₂ production for the year 2015. 4. The data was subsequently disaggregated to produce CFs of grid cells using gridded population maps and gridded income data. First, the urban and rural grid cells were identified using the Global Human Settlement Layer Settlement Model Grid (GHS-SMOD). Then the CF for each region was disaggregated across the grid cells based on the combined purchasing power of the population living within each grid cell. Carbon footprints are usually directly related to income and purchasing power. The population in each cell was multiplied by the mean purchasing power at that location to calculate the overall purchasing power per grid cell. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/aac72a#erlaac72at1). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data on carbon footprints for the top 500 cities in absolute and per capita values are available from the data provider. title: Aqueduct Groundwater Table Decline
description: ### Overview Groundwater table decline measures the average decline of the groundwater table as the average change for the period of study (1990-2014). The result is expressed in centimeters per year (cm/yr). Higher values indicate higher levels of unsustainable groundwater withdrawals. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low risk of decline (<0 cm/yr) to extremely high risk of decline (>8cm/yr). Values are available per aquifer as defined by the [World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP)](https://www.whymap.org/whymap/EN/Home/whymap_node.html). ### Methodology Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB 2), to calculate five indicators. Groundwater table decline is one of those indicators and was calculated by coupling PCR-GLOBWB 2 with MODFLOW to account for lateral groundwater flow processes. This indicator used gridded 14 years of monthly groundwater heads between January 1990 and December 2014. In mountainous areas, very deep groundwater influences the averages in mountainous cells and is not representative. These cells were therefore discarded from the calculations following the method in [de Graaf et al. (2015)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-19-823-2015). After masking the mountainous areas, the results were aggregated to groundwater aquifers derived from the [WHYMAP data set (BGR and UNESCO 2018)](https://www.whymap.org/whymap/EN/Home/whymap_node.html). Next, the monthly results were fit with first-order regression. The slope of this regression line (cm/yr) indicates the existence of a downward (or upward) trend. The trend was assessed using the coefficient of determination (R-squared) and the p value. If R-squared was greater than or equal to 0.9 and the p value was less than or equal to 0.05, the trend was accepted. Finally, raw groundwater table decline values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw groundwater table decline values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 0 cm/yr - Low to medium (1-2): 0 - 2 cm/y - Medium to high (2-3): 2 - 8 cm/yr - High (3-4): 4 - 8cm/yr - Extremely high (4-5): > 8 cm/yr For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](8eafc054-a350-43b5-af61-a64a9a7f8ffe) as a replacement.**_ Freedom in the World is Freedom House’s flagship annual report, assessing the condition of political rights and civil liberties around the world. It is composed of numerical ratings and supporting descriptive texts for 195 countries and 14 territories. Freedom in the World has been published since 1973, allowing Freedom House to track global trends in freedom over more than 40 years. External analysts assess the 209 countries and territories using a combination of on-the-ground research, consultations with local contacts, and information from news articles, nongovernmental organizations, governments, and a variety of other sources. Expert advisers and regional specialists then vet the analysts’ conclusions. The final product represents the consensus of the analysts, advisers, and Freedom House staff. For each country and territory, Freedom in the World analyzes the electoral process, political pluralism and participation, the functioning of the government, freedom of expression and of belief, associational and organizational rights, the rule of law, and personal autonomy and individual rights. A country or territory is assigned 2 ratings (7 to 1)—one for political rights and one for civil liberties—based on its total scores for the political rights and civil liberties questions. Each rating of 1 through 7, with 1 representing the greatest degree of freedom and 7 the smallest degree of freedom, corresponds to a specific range of total scores. The average of a country’s or territory’s political rights and civil liberties ratings is called the Freedom Rating, and it is this figure that determines the status of free (1.0 to 2.5), partly free (3.0 to 5.0), or not free (5.5 to 7.0). title: [Archived] Multidimensional Poverty Index
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](d3486db9-5da4-4aee-a363-f71b643a7ce1) as a replacement.**_ The UN Development Programme (UNDP) compiles the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) as part of its Human Development Report initiative. First published in 2010, the MPI identifies multiple deprivations at the household and individual level in health, education, and standard of living. It uses microdata from household surveys, and—unlike the Inequality-Adjusted Human Development Index—all the indicators needed to construct the measure must come from the same survey. Each person in a given household is classified as poor or nonpoor depending on the weighted number of deprivations his or her household experiences. These data are then aggregated into the national measure of poverty. The MPI reflects both the prevalence of multidimensional deprivation and its intensity—the percentage of simultaneous deprivations poor people experience. It can be used to create a comprehensive picture of people living in poverty and permits comparisons both across countries, regions, and the world and within countries by ethnic group, urban, or rural location, as well as other key household and community characteristics. The MPI offers a valuable complement to income-based poverty measures. Indicators shown in the MPI include the following: (1) health: nutrition and child mortality; (2) education: years of schooling and children enrolled; and (3) standard of living: cooking fuel, toilet, water, electricity, floor, and assets. The MPI is calculated by multiplying the incidence of poverty by the intensity of poverty. The incidence of poverty is the proportion of people considered to experience multidimensional poverty, in other words, that are considered deprived in at least one-third of the MPI's weighted indicators. The intensity of multidimensional poverty is the weighted average number of deprivations poor people experience at the same time. The main data sources of the MPI are the Macro Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) of the Inner City Fund (ICF) and the Multiple Indicators Cluster Survey (MICS) of the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). The 2016 Human Development Report (HDR) presents estimates for 102 developing countries with a combined population of 5.2 billion (72% of the world total). About 1.5 billion people in the countries covered—29% of their entire population—lived in multidimensional poverty between 2005 and 2015. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Average Temperature
description: Annual average temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. title: Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.]( https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Aqueduct Unimproved or No Drinking Water Access
description: ### Overview Unimproved/No drinking water acess reflects the percentage of the population collecting drinking water from an unprotected dug well or spring, or directly from a river, dam, lake, pond, stream, canal, or irrigation canal [(WHO and UNICEF 2017)]([https://washdata.org/data). Specifically, the indicator aligns with the unimproved and surface water categories of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP)—the lowest tiers of drinking water services. Higher values indicate areas where people have less access to safe drinking water supplies. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<2.5%) to extremely high water stress (>20%). The JMP statistics have been disaggregated from the country level to the sub-basin scale (HydroBASIN level 6) using gridded urban and rural population data. ### Methodology Data for this indicator came from the 2015 drinking water access rates published by JMP [(WHO and UNICEF 2017)]([https://washdata.org/data) for urban and rural populations per country. Specifically, this indicator used the unimproved and no surface water statistics. First, country level data were matched to the Aqueduct sub-basin scale using a one-to-one geospatial intersection between Aqueduct sub-basins and countries (henceforth called intersect). Next, the gridded 2010 population data [(van Vuuren et al. 2007)](https://www.pbl.nl/en/publications/2006/DownscalingDriversOfGlobalEnvironmentalChangeScenarios) was parsed into urban and rural classes using a 2010 urban extent data layer [(van Huijstee et al. 2018)](https://www.pbl.nl/en/publications/towards-an-urban-preview). The total urban and rural populations were then summed per intersect. Within each intersect, the urban and rural rates of access were multiplied by the urban and rural populations, respectively, and then were added together to find the number of people with access to unimproved/no drinking water. Results were aggregated up from the intersect scale to the HydroBASIN 6 scale. Within each HydroBASIN 6 sub-basin, the population with access to unimproved/no drinking water was divided by the total population to find the percent of population with access to unimproved/no drinking water. Finally, raw unimproved/no drinking water access values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw unimproved/no drinking water access values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 2.5% - Low to medium (1-2): 2.5 - 5.0% - Medium to high (2-3): 5.0 - 10.0% - High (3-4): 10.0 - 20.0% - Extremely high (4-5): >20.0% For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Minimum Arctic Sea Ice
description: ### Overview The Minimum Arctic Sea Ice dataset shows the annual minimum extent of sea ice in the Arctic for select years between 1980-2020. Arctic sea ice typically reaches its minimum extent in September. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice was present during September for each year. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). This dataset is derived from two products: a near real-time daily dataset and a separate daily dataset that is processed yearly. For the most recent 6-18 months, sea ice extents were derived from near real-time data; all older data was derived from the separate daily dataset. This dataset can be used to understand changes in annual minimum Arctic sea ice extent over the past 40 years. Arctic sea ice extent has been declining since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property – albedo –keeps the polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature and ice melt. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Minimum Arctic Sea Ice was produced from two sources: NASA's [Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0051) and NSIDC’s [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081). Data for the GSFC and NRTSI datasets was collected by the following six sensors: - GSFC data: - [Nimbus-7 Satellite](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987 - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991 - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995 - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007 - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to present - NRTSI data: - DMSP-F18 SSMIS from April 2016 to present The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. Data was collected daily by the SSM/I and SSMIS sensors and on alternate days by the SMMR sensor. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from the ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their average monthly ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Images of sea ice extent were created for each month, with ice shown in light blue. The process was the same for both the NRTSI and GSFC datasets. GSFC data had a tighter quality control than NRTSI data. However, GSFC data is only released once per year. NRTSI data was available at the end of each month, so it was used to produce sea ice extents while GSFC data was being processed. GSFC data replaced NRTSI data once it was available. Thus, data from the most recent 6-18 months was derived from the NRTSI dataset and older data was derived from the GSFC dataset. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a). description: The data layers indicate a district-wise comparison of water resource vulnerability in Madhya Pradesh in the baseline and mid-century based on two different emission scenarios RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5. The analysis is based on a water resources vulnerability index (WRVI) that was arrived at by aggregating and weighing a cross section 8 indicators (such as water availability during different monsoon periods, crop water stress, frequency of drought, flood discharge etc]. According to the analysis the overall water resources vulnerability of Madhya Pradesh districts is projected to increase towards mid-century under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 climate scenarios as compared to current conditions. title: [Archived] Fires (MODIS)
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](20cc5eca-8c63-4c41-8e8e-134dcf1e6d76) as a replacement.**_ The Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Thermal Anomalies/Fire products are primarily derived from MODIS 4 and 11 micrometer radiances. The fire detection strategy is based on absolute detection of a fire (when the fire strength is sufficient to detect) and on detection relative to its background (to account for variability of the surface temperature and reflection by sunlight). The product includes fire occurrence (day/night), fire location, the logical criteria used for the fire selection, detection confidence, fire radiative power, and numerous other layers describing fire pixel attributes. The product distinguishes between fire, no fire, and no observation. Level 3 Daily fire products include 8 separate days of data detailing pixels according to their level of confidence as fires. This information will be used in monitoring the spatial and temporal distribution of fires in different ecosystems, detecting changes in fire distribution, and identifying new fire frontiers, wildfires, and changes in the frequency of the fires or their relative strength. MODIS data on Terra and Aqua are acquired from each platform twice daily at mid-latitudes. These 4 daily MODIS fire observations that are typically acquired serve operational fire management needs while also advancing global monitoring of the fire process and its effects on ecosystems, the atmosphere, and climate. description: The Crop Harvested Area and Production data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE) and the Land Use and Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC). It shows the harvested area, yield and production amount of 175 crops in 206 countries for the year 2000 (average of census data between 1997 and 2003). Harvested area represents the fractional proportion of hectares harvested per gridcell. Production is calculated by multiplying harvested area in hectares and crop yield in tons per hectare. The data were collected from agricultural census and survey information on the areas and yields of 175 crops from the smallest political units reasonably obtainable for 206 countries. Data availability varies for different crops within each country, with most countries having subnational statistics for some crops but national statistics for others. The largest single source of subnational data is Agro-MAPS, a joint project between the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the International Food Policy Research Institute and the Center for Sustainability and the Global Environment. Croplands cover about 15 million km² of the planet and provide the bulk of the food and fiber essential to human well-being. Most global land cover data sets from satellites group croplands into just a few categories, thereby excluding information critical for answering key questions on subjects ranging from biodiversity conservation to food security to biogeochemical cycling. Information about agricultural land use practices like crop selection, yield and fertilizer use is even more limited. These EarthStat data present land use data sets created by combining national, state and county-level census statistics with a recently updated global data set of croplands on a 5 minute by 5 minute (~10 km x 10 km) latitude/longitude grid. description: The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) active fires data (VNP14IMGTDL_NRT) produced by NASA are the latest fire monitoring product of the Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which identifies global fire locations in near-real time. Information is collected from the VIIRS sensor and processed with a fire detection algorithm to flag active fires. Each dot on the map represents the center of a 375-meter pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. This higher resolution enables detection of smaller fires and provides a more reliable estimate of fire perimeters than the previously available MODIS data. The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspots or fire pixels. Fires over the past 24 hours are accessible on this site, and information for older fires is available on the NASA FIRMS website. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. title: Watersheds
description: ### Overview The HydroBASINS dataset depicts watershed boundaries and sub-basin delineations at a global scale. A watershed is an area of land that drains all surface and groundwater to a common body of water. The boundaries of watersheds provide important geospatial units for many applications, but at a global scale there is a lack of high-quality sources for watershed mapping and analysis. The HydroBasins dataset is part of the HydroSHEDS database ([Hydrological data and maps based on SHuttle Elevation Derivatives](http://www.hydrosheds.org)) which provides hydrographic data layers that allow for the derivation of watershed boundaries for any given location based on the near-global, high-resolution [Shuttle Radar Topology Mission](https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/srtm/) digital elevation model. The goal of this product is to provide a seamless global coverage of consistently sized and hierarchically nested sub-basins at different scales (from tens to millions of square kilometers), supported by a coding scheme that allows for analysis of watershed topology such as up- and downstream connectivity. The HydroSHEDS database generates key data layers to support regional and global watershed analyses, hydrological modeling, and freshwater conservation planning at a quality, resolution and extent that has previously been unachievable. Watersheds in this database are delineated at 15 arc-second resolution with a hierarchical sub-basin breakdown. The HydroBASINS product was created in 2013. It was developed on behalf of the World Wildlife Fund US (WWF), with support from and in collaboration with the [EU BioFresh] (http://www.freshwaterbiodiversity.eu/contact/) project, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and McGill University. ### Methodology All HydroBASINS layers were derived from World Wildlife Fund’s [HydroSHEDS data](http://www.hydrosheds.org) based on a grid resolution of 15 arc-seconds (approximately 500 m x 500 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.). An important characteristic of any sub-basin delineation is the sub-basin breakdown, i.e. the decision of when and how to subdivide a larger basin into multiple tributary basins. Standard GIS tools offer the possibility to break out sub-watersheds at any confluence where the inflowing branches (i.e., a tributary and its main stem) exceed a certain size threshold, typically measured by the number of upstream pixels or the upstream catchment area. HydroBASINS divides a basin into two sub-basins at every location where two river branches meet which each have an individual upstream area of at least 100 km². A second critical feature of sub-basin delineations is the way the sub-basins are grouped or coded to allow for the breakout of nested sub-basins at different scales, or to navigate within the sub-basin network from up- to downstream. One of the easiest methods for navigation is to provide the ID of the next downstream object, which allows for moving from object to object in order to traverse the network. As for nesting and topological concepts, the ‘Pfafstetter’ coding system is frequently used due to its relative simplicity and ease of application. The basic principle of the Pfafstetter coding is that a larger basin is sequentially subdivided into 9 smaller units (the 4 largest tributaries, coded with even numbers, and the 5 inter-basins, coded with odd numbers). Thus, the next finer resolution of a sub-basin delineation is achieved at the next Pfafstetter level by adding one digit to the code of the previous level. A more detailed description of the Pfafstetter coding is provided in literature (e.g., [Verdin and Verdin 1999](https://www.bowdoin.edu/~ltoma/teaching/cs3225-GIS/fall16/Project-watershed/papers-watershed/1999-delineate-verdin.pdf)). The HydroBASINS product provides levels 1 to 12 globally. Level 1 distinguishes 9 continents. Level 2 splits each continent into up to 9 large sub-units. Level 3 corresponds to the largest river basins for each continent. From Level 4 onwards, the breakdown follows the Pfafstetter concept. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.hydrosheds.org/images/inpages/HydroBASINS_TechDoc_v1c.pdf) ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Delineations for all Pfafstetter levels (1-12) by region can be downloaded from the the source. A version of this dataset with inserted lakes as well as data for void-filled elevation, hydrologically conditioned elevation, drainage directions, flow accumulation, river networks, basin outlines, lake shorelines, and other hydro-environmental variables is also available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/wat_068_rw0_watersheds). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. title: Current and Projected Food Insecurity
description: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Elevation
description: Global 30 Arc-Second Elevation (GTOPO30) is a global digital elevation model (DEM) with a horizontal grid spacing of 30 arc seconds (approximately 1 kilometer). GTOPO30 was derived from several raster and vector sources of topographic information. Completed in late 1996, GTOPO30 was developed over a three year period through a collaborative effort led by staff at the U.S. Geological Survey's Center for Earth Resources Observation and Science (EROS). title: Coping Strategies for Food Insecurity
description: The World Food Programme Mobile Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping unit uses phone-based surveys to create a Coping Strategies Index for regions at risk of needing food aid or market assistance. The CSI is based on the many possible answers to a single question: "What do you do when you don't have adequate food, and don't have the money to buy food?" An advantage of the CSI is that it is often quicker and easier to observe coping strategies than actual food consumption profiles. The reduced CSI (rCSI) only accounts for coping strategies that are nearly universal in the areas where the WFP works. The CSI and rCSI have been shown to be well correlated with future food insecurity and are therefore useful metrics for organizations that offer food aid and market support. Designing a full CSI requires that program analysts engage focus groups in the area of interest to determine the list of unique coping strategies used by locals. The rCSI has been developed based on the most common coping strategies observed in the past CSI implementations. The rCSI has been shown to correlate nearly as well with food insecurity as the original, context-specific CSI, but it is easier and faster to create. The rCSI has the additional benefit of being comparable across geographic regions and cultural contexts, which is useful for developing objective methods for the allocation and geographic targeting of aid resources. There are 2 basic types of coping strategy: * Changing short-term consumption * Longer-term alteration of income earning or food production patterns, including asset sales The rCSI includes the following strategies and associated (severities): * Eating less-preferred foods (1.0) * Borrowing food/money from friends and relatives (2.0) * Limiting portions at mealtime (1.0) * Limiting adult intake (3.0) * Reducing the number of meals per day (1.0) The results of the rCSI can be incorporated into early warning systems to address acute food insecurity before it develops, or as part of postdistribution monitoring systems to evaluate the success of emergency and long-term interventions. title: Fishery Production
description: ### Overview The Fishery Production dataset on Resource Watch shows annual time series data of national aquaculture, capture, and total fishery production beginning in 1950. The data displayed cover capture fishery production related to catch of fish, crustaceans, molluscs and other aquatic animals taken for commercial, industrial, recreational and subsistence purposes from inland, brackish and marine waters. The data also cover aquaculture fishery production related to the farming of aquatic organisms including fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants. Quantities are given in metric tons (=1000 kg). The fisheries and aquaculture sector contributes significantly to food security and nutrition, especially in some of the world’s most food-limited regions, while simultaneously supporting the livelihood of hundreds of millions of people around the world. It is critical to ensure fisheries are managed responsibly and sustainably around the world. This requires standardized, reliable and up-to-date information on fishery production and supply chain, as well as the consideration of social and economic aspects, for making sound policy and assessing the performance of responsible fisheries and aquaculture management systems. Furthermore, timely, trustworthy data are crucial for demonstrating progress towards the [2030 UN Agenda for Sustainable Development](https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/development-agenda/). Attaining the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) will require a solid framework of indicators and statistical data to monitor progress, inform policy and ensure accountability of all stakeholders. The FAO works to achieve food security for all, and as the custodian agency of four indicators under SDG14, the FAO has an obligation to accelerate the global momentum to secure healthy and productive oceans. Underpinning these efforts is the need to rely on high quality national, regional and global statistics, while ensuring these data are freely accessible to all. To meet this need, the FAO provides the only source of global statistics on capture fisheries and aquaculture production—a unique global asset for sector analysis and monitoring. ### Methodology Data on Fisheries and Aquaculture Production are sourced annually from relevant national offices concerned with fishery statistics. Information is collected by means of a system of standardized forms, which list for each country the relative species items and fishing areas breakdown. In the case of some "aquatic products," data are also obtained from trade associations or other specialized international organizations to which data are also submitted. In this way the statistics are reviewed by subject matter specialists. Data concerning the nominal catch of certain major groups are generally reviewed in collaboration with the regional agency concerned. For example, data on tuna provided by the national correspondents are often replaced by the "best scientific estimates" produced by regional bodies collecting tuna catch statistics. For the period 1950–1995, capture and aquaculture were compiled together in the total production statistics. However, capture and aquaculture production quantities have since been extended back to 1950. Capture data relate to the nominal catches of fish, crustaceans, molluscs, aquatic mammals, other aquatic animals, residues (used for fishmeal and fish oil production) and plants. Catches from capture production are taken for commercial, industrial, recreational and subsistence purposes from inland, brackish and marine waters. Data include all quantities caught and landed for both food and feed purposes but exclude discards. Aquaculture data relate to the farming of aquatic organisms including fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants. Farming implies some form of intervention in the rearing process to enhance production, such as regular stocking, feeding, protection from predators, etc. Farming also implies individual or corporate ownership of the stock being cultivated. For statistical purposes, aquatic organisms which are harvested by an individual or corporate body which has owned them throughout their rearing period contribute to aquaculture while aquatic organisms which are exploitable by the public as a common property resource, with or without appropriate licenses, are the harvest of fisheries. Catches of fish, crustaceans and molluscs are expressed in live weight, that is, the nominal weight of the aquatic organisms at the time of capture. The harvest of aquatic plants is given in wet weight. Data are given in metric tons (=1000 kg), except those for whales, seals and crocodiles, which are given in numbers. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.fao.org/cwp-on-fishery-statistics/handbook/capture-fisheries-statistics/en/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows FAO yearbook data for [ocean-sourced dietary energy and protein supply](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/foo061rw0-Blue-Food-Supply). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for species and fishing areas as well as data on commodities, trade, catches, number of fishers, and consumption are provided by the FAO fisheries division. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Food Price Spikes
description: ### Overview The Alert for Price Spikes (ALPS) dataset tracks the current prices of key staple food commodities and compares them to expected prices, which are calculated based on seasonal trends. An ALPS value is assigned to a given commodity at a particular market based on how much its current price differs from the expected price. This value is used to categorize a commodity’s price into one of four categories: normal, stress, alert, or crisis. Food prices on a local market often correlated with food security crises. Food price spikes can have devastating impacts for rural households in developing countries since they spend a large percentage of income on food. ALPS serves three main purposes for decision-making. First, it can serve as a price monitoring tool that allows users to identify price abnormalities. Second, ALPS can generate early warning information that enables users to prepare and act to reduce harm to households most vulnerable to food price fluctuations. Third, ALPS can trigger contingency planning by anticipating food price crises. The ALPS dataset is generated by the World Food Programme (WFP) and monitors markets spanning more than 60 countries. The time period over which prices have been tracked varies by location, but certain markets have food price data as early as 1994. The data is updated monthly for markets that are actively being monitored. ### Methodology Seasonal price trends were determined through reference to monthly commodity prices recorded in the WFP's Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping (VAM) Food and Commodity Price dataset. This dataset was collected by WFP country offices, national government agencies, and partner organizations. The ALPS indicator level was calculated in four steps: - **Estimation of seasonal price trends**: The seasonal price trend was calculated using a linear regression of market price data over the entire period for which data was available. Both the long-term trend and monthly fluctuations, related to the production or demand of a commodity, were included in the regression. - **Calculation of the difference between market price and estimated price**: The difference between the observed price and the expected price based on seasonal trends was calculated for each month. - **Calculation of the ALPS indicator considering price volatility**: Each month’s difference was divided by the standard deviation of the differences over all of the recorded months, producing the value of the ALPS indicator. - **Categorization of the ALPS indicator**: Based on the ALPS indicator value, markets were assigned to one of four situations: (1) Normal: ALPS < 0.25; (2) Stress: 0.25 ≤ ALPS < 1; (3) Alert: 1 ≤ ALPS < 2; (4) Crisis: ALPS ≥ 2. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Glacier Locations
description: The GLIMS: Global Glacier Database managed by the NSIDC is an international collaborative project that includes more than 60 institutions worldwide. Its goal is to create this globally comprehensive inventory of land ice including measurements of glacier area, geometry, surface velocity, and snow line elevation. To perform these analyses, the GLIMS project uses satellite data, primarily from the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) and the Landsat Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+), as well as historical information derived from maps and aerial photographs. The analysis results are submitted to the GLIMS database at the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) in Boulder, CO. The GLIMS database is designed to be a logical extension of the World Glacier Inventory (WGI) of the World Glacier Monitoring Service (WGMS) and stores the full complement of the WGMS-defined glacier characteristics. Each analysis received by the GLIMS team at the NSIDC is ingested into the GLIMS Glacier Database. New glacier data are continually being added to the database. title: Coral Reef Bleaching Alerts
description: The Coral Reef Watch (CRW) program of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAH) produces this daily 5 km product of coral reef bleaching alert areas, allowing direct monitoring of 95% of global coral reefs. This 7-day composite product shows the maximum stress level that an ocean pixel has experienced due to high sea surface temperature (SST) during the most recent 7 consecutive days, and are dated on the last day of the period. These data are used as the core of NOAA's CRW coral bleaching management program. These coral bleaching alerts are derived from the NOAA National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service (NESDIS) 5 km Geo-Polar Blended Night-Only SST Analysis. Long-term satellite data of SST is used to define the "usual" SST for a given grid cell. This is taken to be the maximum monthly mean SST over that grid cell. For example, if September is the month with the hottest average SST, the September mean SST will be taken as that grid cell's "usual" value. A HotSpot is then defined as temperatures that are higher than this average. A Degree Heating Week is defined as a grid cell being week degree C hotter than usual for a period of one week. The Bleaching Alert Levels are defined as below. This product shows the maximum bleaching alert level that a grid square has reached in the past 7 consecutive days. Stress Level Definition Effect No Stress HotSpot <= 0 Bleaching Watch 0 < HotSpot < 1 Bleaching Warning 1 <= HotSpot and 0 < DHW < 4 Possible Bleaching Bleaching Alert Level 1 1 <= HotSpot and 4 <= DHW < 8 Bleaching Likely Bleaching Alert Level 2 1 <= HotSpot and 8 <= DHW Mortality Likely Full technical details on the types of satellites used, data collected, and analyses performed are available at the following sites: http://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/6/11/11579 and https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/methodology/methodology.php#sst. title: Anthropogenic Biomes
description: Anthropogenic Biomes, also known as Anthromes, are defined as “the globally significant ecological patterns created by sustained interactions between humans and ecosystems.” The Anthropogenic Biomes data set illustrates historical transformations within the terrestrial biosphere, land-based regions occupied by living organisms, illustrated through the changes in the anthromes. The data set reclassifies the terrestrial biosphere into 19 anthrome classes at 5-degree resolution for the years 1700, 1800, 1900, and 2000 to illustrate historical changes. The classification used a rule-based anthrome classification model based on human population density and land use data. The transformation of terrestrial biomes is assessed by comparing potential natural vegetation maps with anthrome maps using overlay analysis and other analytical geographic information system (GIS) software tools. The anthrome classes included in this data set are urban (urban, mixed settlements), villages (rice villages, irrigated villages, rainfed villages, pastoral villages), croplands (residential irrigated croplands, residential rainfed croplands, populated rainfed croplands, remote croplands), rangelands (residential rangelands, populated rangelands, remote rangelands), forested (residential woodlands, populated woodlands, remote woodlands, inhabited treeless and barren lands), and woodlands (wild woodlands, wild treeless and barren lands). The Anthropogenic Biomes data set was created by the Anthromes Working Group. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Satellite Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: O₃ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of ozone (O₃) densities in the total atmospheric column. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of O₃ found between Earth’s surface and the top of the atmosphere. The O₃ density is reported with units of moles of O₃ per square meter of air (mol/m²). Unlike stratospheric ozone, which forms naturally in the upper atmosphere and protects us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays, ground-level (or tropospheric) ozone is created through the interactions of man-made (and natural) emissions of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides in the presence of heat and sunlight. Cars and gasoline-burning engines are large sources of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). VOCs also come from consumer products such as paints, insecticides, and cleaners as well as industrial solvents and chemical manufacturing. High concentrations of ozone near ground level can be harmful to people, animals, crops, and other materials. Ozone can irritate the respiratory system, causing coughing and irritation. Ozone can aggravate pre existing respiratory problems like asthma, emphysema, and bronchitis and reduce the immune system's ability to fight off infections. Additionally, it can inflame and damage cells that line the lungs. It is possible for ozone to cause irreparable lung damage. These effects can be worse in children and exercising adults. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as O₃, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [carbon monoxide (CO)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). ### Methodology The TROPOMI O₃ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. O₃ data was collected by determining the amount of radiation reflected by the troposphere in the UV Huggins bands (325-335 nanometers) spectral range of the solar spectrum. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that O₃ molecules produce in the atmosphere. The O₃ data collected using this method was then input into the GODFIT (GOME Direct-FITting) algorithm, created by the European Space Agency. Along with O₃ data, the following information was input into GODFIT: - Relative profile of O₃ and sulfur dioxide (SO₂) in the atmosphere for a given region - Estimated surface albedo for the region - Solar/viewing geometry and geo-location of the S5P satellite - Surface pressure, elevation map, snow and ice maps for the earth’s surface, ozone temperature, cloud cover/pressure profiles, and the absorbing aerosol index for the tropospheric column being measured SO₂ profiles were required as SO₂ converts to sulfuric acid in the atmosphere and blocks incoming solar radiation. This interferes with O₃ readings by TROPOMI. The results from GODFIT were analyzed with the convective-cloud-differential method (CCD) combined with cloud measurement data to produce the final dataset. The final result produced was vertical total column density of O₃ (mol/m²). The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Ozone (O₃) Total Column”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [carbon monoxide] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). title: Cooling Degree Days
description: A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts. This data set shows CDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages.
