description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for fine particulate matter (PM2.5). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources. PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even get into the bloodstream. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of health problems, including: premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, and increased respiratory symptoms. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are most likely to be affected by particle pollution exposure. OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1). ### Methodology The fine particulate matter (PM2.5) station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria: 1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site. 2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region. 3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours. After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour. City Expansion Index
description: ### Overview The city expansion index dataset shows outward and upward urban growth in 377 cities globally that have a population of over 1 million residents. Outward growth is the horizontal expansion of buildings and upward growth is the vertical expansion of buildings. The final dataset was normalized into comparable values called the Upward Growth Index and Outward Growth Index. A higher expansion index value means more growth is occurring. The dataset uses remote sensing data collected between 2000 and 2014. This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the World Resources Report (WRR) Towards a More Equal City. It is intended to highlight regional trends in urban expansion and differences in urban structure within and between cities. Ultimately, it can be used to help governments understand how urban expansion can be managed in a way that achieves more equitable access to core services for the under-served while bringing wider economic and environmental benefits to cities. For the dataset to paint a complete picture it should ideally be used in conjunction with a matching dataset on the socioeconomic information of the city. ### Methodology This dataset was created using a combination of remote sensing data to determine upward and outward expansion in cities with a metropolitan population greater than 1 million. Remote sensing data was collected from mean summer backscatter power ratio (PR) from NASA's SeaWinds microwave scatterometer (Ku-band, 13.4 GHz) and built-up area from the multitemporal Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL). The data showed the outward growth of urban built-up areas between 2000 and 2014 measured from the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) and upward growth between 2001 and 2009 measured using the power ratio (PR) from NASA’s SeaWinds microwave scatterometer. Each dataset was reprocessed to have the same spatial resolution of 0.05 degrees (about 5.6 km at the equator). To determine which cities had a metropolitan population greater than 1 million, Landscan data created by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory was combined with the Oxford Economics database to create a combined dataset of 377 cities. Researchers overlayed an 11x11 pixel grid (121 total pixels) over each city using the dataset Populated Places from Natural Earth to create a unified boundary to measure the cities growth. The 11x11 grids were extracted and all grid cells with a built up value less than 20 percent were masked in GHSL. Total upward and outward growth were then calculated using the remaining pixels for each city by using a cluster analysis to group each pixel into similar urban growth patterns and structures. Finally, the values were converted into the upward urban growth index and outward urban growth index to allow for comparison of the values across cities. The final dataset was presented in raster format at a spatial resolution of 0.28 degrees (20.98 square kilometers at the equator). title: Projected Change in Heating Degree Days (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. HDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is below 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual HDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. HDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for heating buildings. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual HDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily HDDs were calculated by subtracting daily average temperature values from the baseline temperature of 65°F. If the daily average temperature was above 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual HDD was calculated by summing all daily HDD values over a given year. Annual HDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in heating degree days. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Historical Sea Ice Medians
description: ### Overview The Historical Sea Ice Medians dataset shows monthly median sea ice extent over the period of 1981-2010. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments for both the Arctic and Antarctic regions. Satellite data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Gridded ice concentration estimates were used to define the ice edge position that is typical for each month. This dataset shows the maximum (blue line) and minimum (yellow line) sea ice extent, and the typical sea ice extent for each month in between. In the Arctic, sea ice normally reaches its maximum extent in March and its minimum extent in September. Antarctic sea ice extent peaks in September and reaches its minimum in February. The lines in this dataset represent how sea ice expands and retreats between its maximum and minimum extent. This dataset is the [baseline](https://nsidc.org/data/noaa/baseline-change) for sea ice index products from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Climate baselines are used as a historical reference to current trends and anomalies. A three-decade time period is ideal because it averages out short-term variability. This dataset can be used to understand how polar sea ice extent and melting season are changing. Antarctic sea ice behaves differently than Arctic sea ice, largely because the two regions have different land-ocean configurations. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. Arctic sea ice extent has declined since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property – albedo – keeps the polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature and ice melt. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. Comparing current sea ice extent data to this baseline dataset can help define the rates and locations of sea ice retreat. The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/). ### Methodology Historical Sea Ice Medians were generated from data collected by five sensors: - [Nimbus-7](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987 - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991 - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995 - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007 - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to December 2017 The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. The SMMR sensor collected data on alternate days and the SSM/I and SSMIS sensor collected data on a daily basis. Daily satellite measurements were averaged each month to eliminate errors and smooth variations caused by short-term weather conditions. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Median ice extents were calculated by applying the 15% cutoff to all gridded concentration data for each month between 1981 and 2010. Cells that classified as ice more than 50% of the time from 1981-2010 were designated as ice; cells that classified as ice less than 50% of the time were designated as water. This was done on a monthly basis: for example, the data from every January from 1981-2010 was analyzed together to create a single January dataset. Each month’s gridded concentration data was mapped and a contour line was drawn to mark the ice edge. This contour line represents the median sea ice extent. Because the sea ice extent varies considerably from year to year, the median extent is a better representation of the sea ice extent over time. The workflow was applied to both the Arctic and Antarctic regions. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: ### Overview The Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) delivers a global Land Cover product at 100-meter spatial resolution (CGLS-LC100) on an annual basis from 2015-2019. Each pixel value corresponds to a different type (class) of physical coverage of the Earth's surface, e.g. forests, grasslands, croplands, lakes, wetlands. The classifications follow the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (UN-FAO) Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) scheme. Resource watch displays 11 discrete LCCS classifications, with all forests grouped into open or closed classes. Land cover plays a major role in the climate and biogeochemistry of the Earth system. Understanding patterns in land use and transitions of land cover classes over time is crucial to understand, monitor, and manage a number of processes at global level. Therefore, accurate and spatially detailed maps on land cover and land use are relevant to a broad range of issues including deforestation, desertification, urbanization, land degradation, loss of biodiversity and ecosystem functions, water resource management, agriculture and food security, urban and regional development, and climate change and are critical to make informed policy development, planning, and resource management decisions. The Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) is a component of the Land Monitoring Core Service (LMCS) of Copernicus, the European flagship programme on Earth Observation. The Global Land Service systematically produces a series of qualified bio-geophysical products on the status and evolution of the land surface, at global scale and at mid to low spatial resolution, complemented by the constitution of long term time series. The products are used to monitor the vegetation, the water cycle, the energy budget and the terrestrial cryosphere. ### Methodology For the global land cover 100-meter resolution data, the main inputs are PROBA-V satellite observations, organized into millions of Sentinel-2 equivalent tiles of 110x110-kilometers. These satellite observations are put through an algorithm, that includes: - pre-processing, sensor specific data cleaning, and outlier screening - data fusion between the 5-day 100-meter resolution and daily 300-meter resolution data; - extraction of 183 metrics, including the base reflectances, vegetation indicators, time series harmonics and descriptive statistics; - the use of 168K training points, collected at 10-meter resolution, from GeoWIKI’s crowd-sourcing, for year 2015 - the use of well-established, external datasets for the shoreline masking, ecological regionalisation, built-up (urban) cover, permanent and seasonal water cover, arctic vegetation, weather and topography; supervised classification and regression. The classified metrics are calculated over a three year period (epoch), in three processing modes: - base maps for epoch 2015, that serves as reference for the classifier and regression models, - consolidated maps (epochs 2016, 2017 and 2018) with full years of prior and pastor data and - the near-real time (nrt, 2019) maps with one year prior and only three months pastor data. The final maps are validated using an independent set of 21,700 validation points, also sourced from Geo-WIKI. For the full documentation, please see the source [user manual](https://land.copernicus.eu/global/sites/cgls.vito.be/files/products/CGLOPS1_PUM_LC100m-V3_I3.4.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows 11 of the 23 discrete LCCS classifications from the CGLS Land Cover Product. The 12 original forest classes are shown as two classes, open and closed. The ocean and unknown classes are not displayed. Historical data on global land cover from 1992 to 2019 can be found on Resource Watch [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc068brw2-Global-Land-Cover-IPCC-Classification). The products are provided as single-layer, internally compressed GeoTIFF files, per 20x20 degree on the [Land Cover viewer](https://lcviewer.vito.be/), as global files on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/communities/copernicus-land-cover?page=1&size=20), and analyzed on [Google Earth Engine](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/COPERNICUS_Landcover_100m_Proba-V-C3_Global). The annual LC product also includes data for cover fractions (%) for the 10 base classes, an indicator to distinguish forest types, an indicator for the input Data Density, and a change confidence layer (after 2015) are available in the data from the provider. The Land Cover viewer also shows annual maps of change occurrence and of change processes. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. title: Irrigated Crop Water Requirement and Withdrawal
description: The Irrigated Water Requirement and Water Withdrawal data set is prepared by FAO AQUASTAT as part of its Irrigation Water Use study. The data can be used to estimate the amount of irrigation water needed to satisfy crop water demand and compare this with the amount of irrigation water actually used. This provides a measure of a country's shortfall in available irrigation water or irrigation infrastructure. The irrigated water requirement is calculated as irrigation consumptive water use (ICU), which is a function of potential crop evapotranspiration (ETc), effective precipitation (P), and change in soil moisture (DS): ICU = ETc - P - DS Written another way, the irrigation consumptive water use at a point in time (ICU(t)) can be represented as the difference between the potential crop evapotranspiration at time t (ETc(t)) and the actual crop evapotranspiration under nonirrigated conditions at time t (ETa(t)): ICU(t) = ETc(t) - ETa(t) The potential crop evapotranspiration of a grid cell is influenced by certain climatic conditions, such as solar radiation, wind speeds at 2 m, and daily temperatures, among others. The reference evapotranspiration (ETo(t)), determined by the FAO Penman-Monteith equations) in a given area at a given time is the amount of water that would be released into the atmosphere through evapotranspiration if the entire ground surface were covered in a certain crop, typically taken to be grass 12 cm tall, and there were no limits on available water. Each other crop (c) has a crop factor (Kc) that can be used to scale the ETo(t) to obtain ETc(t): ETc(t) = Kc x ETo(t) 118 out of 165 countries in the study report the volume of water used for irrigation to FAO AQUASTAT. For the remaining 47 countries, AQUASTAT developed a method for calculating regional (r) correction ratios (CRr) that relate the total irrigation water requirements for countries in that region (IWRr) to the total irrigation water withdrawn for countries in that region (IWWr). CRr = IWRr / IWWrWhen reliable data on a country's IWW (IWWc) are not available, these values are replaced using the IWRr and CRr of the country's relevant surrounding region: IWWc = IWRr / CRr Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Projected Change in Frost Free Season U.S. (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

description: Annual average high temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. title: Climate Hazard Indicators (Annual minimum temperatures - mean) Historical and SSP scenarios - Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
description: ### Overview The dataset includes five major climatic indicators viz. annual values for minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), total precipitation (mm/year), and the number of rainy days (represented as integers) for two Indian states, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. It features decadal averages from 2020-2100 for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), including SSP5-8.5, which reflects a high emissions scenario, and SSP2-4.5, representing moderate challenges to both mitigation and adaptation. Additionally, the dataset provides historical data for all the five indicators averaged over the period from 2005 to 2014. ### Methodology **Pre-Processing**: The decadal time periods were labeled as follows: 2020-2029 as 2020, 2030-2039 as 2030, 2040-2049 as 2040, 2050-2059 as 2050, 2060-2069 as 2060, 2070-2079 as 2070, 2080-2089 as 2080, and 2090-2099 as 2090. **Layers of interest**: Annual averages of minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), Annual total precipitation (mm/year), and the annual total number of rainy days (represented as integers). **Data**: The ERA5 reanalysis dataset (ECMWF 2022), a satellite data product of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts with a spatial resolution of 31 kilometers (km), is used as a reference dataset. The ensemble of downscaled daily time series outputs from global climate models (GCMs). These time series include the historical years covered by the observation time series as well as the specified future years of interest. We have used the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 product, which includes outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models at approximately 25 km spatial resolution. ### Estimation Methods Out of the 35 models, we select the top 3 climate models that perform best for a specific weather variable in a particular geographic region, and present the ensemble mean of these models. The ERA5 dataset is used as a reference, and the comparison is made for the historical period between 1980 and 2014. After selecting the models, we apply a calibration/bias correction procedure to the future time series of the models. This involves aligning the model's frequency distribution with the historical data by shifting the percentiles of the model's distribution. For instance, if the 20th percentile of the model data corresponds to the 30th percentile of the observations, then the 30th percentile of the calibrated model data will match the 20th percentile of the uncalibrated model data. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Wong, T., and P Switzer. 2023. 'Estimating future local climate hazard probabilities.' Technical Note. Washington, DC: World Resources Institute. Available online at: doi.org/10.46830/writn.22.00074.v2. ### Description of the Layers **Annual Maximum Temperature (℃)**: The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Minimum Temperature (℃)**: The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Mean Temperature (℃)**: The daily mean temperature is calculated by averaging the daily minimum and maximum temperatures. The annual mean temperature is obtained by averaging the daily mean temperatures over the course of a year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Total Precipitation (mm/year)**: The daily precipitation values are summed over the entire year to calculate the annual total precipitation. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. **Annual Rainy Days (represented as integers)**: A rainy day is defined as a day with precipitation exceeding 2.5 mm (as per the India Meteorological Department). The total number of rainy days in a year is calculated by summing the rainy days throughout the year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years. ### Visualizing the Data The data is provided at a 25-km resolution and is presented as a raster with a time slider with a separate layer for each variable. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shade (indicating low values) to darker shade (representing higher values). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](d6e42176-90c4-429d-8cae-7619c545a458) as a replacement.**_ The European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC) and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) created a 250-meter resolution population grid. Residential population estimates for 1975, 1990, 2000 and 2015 were generated by disaggregating census or administrative unit population data and re-mapping them to grid cells. The distribution and density of built-up area (from the Global Human Settlement Layer) informed the re-mapping of the population data. The model used raster-based density mapping relying on the Global Human Settlement – Built-Up Area data to define the distribution of people and inform the respective density. The Built-Up grid is the distribution of built-up areas displayed as the proportion of occupied area within each cell. Population estimates came from country-based census data and administrative polygons with estimated residential populations. Population grids were created using a volume-preserving density mapping approach: given population data and built-up area data: A. If the polygon generates 250 meter cells and contains built-up area data, disaggregate the population in proportion to density of built-up area; B. If the polygon generates 250-meter cells and does not contain built-up area data, disaggregate the population using areal weighting; C. If the polygon does not generate its own 250-meter cell, convert polygon to point (centroid within), sum al points within a cell, and sum to a mosaic of A and B. Option C was required because some populated source zones (polygons) were smaller than a 250 x 250 meter cell. This process preserved the full resolution of the Gridded Population of the World data set. All data came from the respective years. description: ### Overview The Air Quality: NO₂ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) density in the troposphere. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of NO₂ between Earth’s surface and the top of the troposphere. The NO₂ density is reported with units of moles of NO₂ per square meter of air (mol/m²). Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is one of the most common compounds in the nitrogen oxides (NOx) group. Other nitrogen oxides include nitric acid (HNO₃) and nitric oxide (NO). NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides, meaning if NO₂ is present it is likely other nitrogen oxides are as well. NO₂ is primarily created by the burning of fuel, which can be from cars, trucks and buses, power plants, and off-road equipment. Breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the human respiratory system. Acute exposures can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms, like coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing. Longer chronic exposures to elevated concentrations of NO₂ may contribute to the development of asthma and potentially increase susceptibility to respiratory infections. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system. The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as NO₂, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). ### Methodology The TROPOMI NO₂ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. The data was retrieved and analyzed using a 3 step process. 1. Total NO₂ slant column density was determined from radiance and irradiance spectra measured by TROPOMI. It was analyzed using a Differential Optical Absorption Spectroscopy (DOAS) method. NO₂ slant column density is the amount of NO₂ found along an average path taken by photons traveling from the sun to the satellite sensor. 2. Slant column density data was then separated into stratospheric and tropospheric categories based on information coming from the satellite’s data assimilation system. Stratospheric data was then removed from the dataset. 3. Tropospheric slant column density was converted into tropospheric vertical column density and the average NO₂ density for the entire vertical column was calculated. This was determined by applying an appropriate air mass factor (AMF) and actual, daily information on the vertical distribution of NO₂ calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model. The altitude-dependent AMF used depended on the satellite geometry, terrain height, cloud fraction and height, and surface albedo. The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Total Column”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. description: ### Overview This dataset shows the paths cyclones have followed and their intensities, from 1980 to the present. The data includes information on tropical cyclones by location, ocean basin, scale, name, wind speed, and other intensity parameters. The International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) is run by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). According to NOAA, a tropical cyclone is a weather event that produces rotating clouds, high winds, and thunderstorms. These cyclones are called hurricanes in the North Atlantic, central North Pacific, and eastern North Pacific. Elsewhere they are called typhoons or tropical typhoons. The disruptions from tropical cyclones have significant impacts on human life, property, and ecology. By compiling data in one place, this dataset can support scientific research efforts in understanding the distribution, frequency, and intensity of tropical cyclones, and assist emergency managers with disaster mitigation efforts. ### Methodology Researchers obtained this data from various agencies either directly through agency websites or via personal communication. The data originated from satellite observations. The data files were then converted into a common format with two general steps. To solve the double-reporting issue with various data sources, step 1 identified each unique storm with an algorithm based on the storm’s position. Step 2 harmonized intensity estimates across data sources so that the intensity parameters are comparable. In cases of different sources having different positions and intensities, researchers calculated the average values from all available reports. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/pdf/10.1175/2009BAMS2755.1). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Water Change
description: ### Overview The global annual surface water percent and surface water dynamics maps were created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory, and the data is available at 30 m spatial resolution, globally, from 2000 to 2020. The GLAD laboratory classified all available Landsat 5, 7, and 8 scenes. Each scene was classified per pixel to identify land, water, and ground obscured by cloud, shadow, haze, or ice. Land and water observations were summed by month from all available images. These counts were aggregated to estimate the annual temporal percent of the year each pixel had water presence, resulting in values of 0-100, and pixels with no observations a no-data value of 255. In order to characterize the type of surface water dynamic over the 21 years, the annual water percent was estimated for each year and temporally filtered to provide greater consistency. A series of rules were applied to this time series to characterize it into permanent land or water, stable seasonal, unidirectional loss or gain, temporary dry or wet period, and high-frequency transitions between annual states of water and land. The pixels that experienced temporary dry or wet periods and high frequency transitions were mapped as variable water. The Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery is the primary data source, and the land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally. ### Methodology Open surface water, or simply water, is defined as inland water that covers ≥50% of a pixel and is not obscured by objects on or above the water surface, for example, forest canopy, floating aquatic vegetation, bridges, or ice. The analysis had three major steps: (1) classify every Landsat scene 1999-2020; (2) create an annual percent water time-series; and (3) characterize the time-series into various dynamics classes. All Landsat 5, 7, and 8 scenes from 2000-2020 were classified into land, water, and unusable data. Due to the diversity of reflectance patterns for open surface water targets, an ensemble of hierarchical, bagged classification trees were used to discriminate clear observations from those contaminated by cloud, shadow, and ice and to discriminate water from land. These classification trees were developed from a training set of 150-180 fully labeled scenes per sensor [(Potapov et al., 2015)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2014.11.027). The classification models utilize all the Landsat bands, normalized difference ratios of each pair of spectral bands, and 3x3 pixel spatial averages of all bands and ratios, as well as, utilize topographic inputs of elevation and derived slope, aspect, and hillshade data. The annual water percent time series was derived from the counts of water and land observations. To account for intra-annual variation in clear observation frequency (e.g. fewer observations in the far north in winter due to low sun elevations or in tropical monsoon environments due to high cloud cover), the percent of land and water observations flagged as water (water / (water + land)) was first calculated per meteorological season (December-February, March-May, June-August, September-November) of each year. Then the average water percent of the seasons with data was assigned as the annual water percent. Temporal filters and manual masks were applied to remove noise and omission/commission errors. An inter-annual water dynamics model was developed to characterize and visualize the dynamics of water presence 2000-2020. The annual water percent time series was first smoothed using a 3-year mean moving window, and the range and mean were calculated per pixel. Pixels with a range of ≤33% and a mean of ≤10% or ≥90% were labeled permanent land and water, respectively, providing a stable target with low sensitivity to possible omission or commission effects due to image artifacts or atmospheric conditions. Change pixels were identified as pixels with a range of ≥50%, and all other pixels labeled as stable seasonal, characterized by having little or no inter-annual variation in water presence and consistent intra-annual variation. By an analysis of all local maxima and minima in the time-series, pixels labeled as change were further characterized into the following main change types: gain, loss, dry period (water-land-water), wet period (land-water-land), and high-frequency (3 or more) land-water transitions. For more details, please refer to Pickens et al. [(2020)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rse.2020.111792). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Extent](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/50634b51-ea2e-4cc1-9e4b-8f26a389a301), [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Tree Height Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/64a3e126-000b-46fb-aaf4-8ac765a8263b), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), [Built-Up Area Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e6a3f803-1222-46c2-8e6c-0ae94b3d80c8), and [Land Cover Map](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/06e734af-66f0-4c3e-ac71-1b99f3cbfe1d). title: Economic Capacity Categorization of Cities
description: ### Overview The Economic Capacity Categorization of Cities dataset shows the projected change in population and categorization of 769 cities based on their economic capacity to meet urban service needs between 2015 and 2030. Cities are categorized into four groups based on their current economic strength, projected population, and economic growth. Gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is used as an indicator of a city’s income. The four categories used in the dataset are: struggling, emerging, thriving, and stabilizing cities. This categorization can help identify cities that will likely face the greatest challenges in providing urban services in the future. It will also assist in locating cities that have the opportunity to avoid locking in unsustainable patterns of urban development. The dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) with data from Oxford Economics' Global Cities 2030 database in conjunction with the United Nations World Urbanization Prospects and the World Bank's World Development Indicators. Oxford Economics’ Global Cities 2030 service has been developed to explore market trends and opportunities among the world’s largest 750 cities. The service provides city (and corresponding national) annual historic estimates (back to 2000 where possible) and forecasts (to 2030) to support business decision making and strategy, research analysis, urban planning, and client consultation and engagements. This classification of cities can help to understand the challenges that cities will face in the years ahead. WRI believes that the pattern of urbanization will change in the future, and a new vision of how to build and manage cities is crucial in developing cities where everyone can live, move, and thrive. ### Methodology The Economic Capacity Categorization of Cities dataset was created by reviewing patterns in income, projected population, and economic growth data. The cities included in the dataset were from Oxford Economics’ Global Cities 2030 database and have at least 400,000 inhabitants or were deemed “strategically” important, like country capitals. Researchers collected data on current GDP per capita as a means of understanding a city’s current economic strength. This data was combined with projected growth in GDP per capita between 2015 and 2030 relative to the projected growth in urban population over the same time period. WRI proposed that these are good measures of how well a city’s resource base can serve its population into the future. These two measures were used to distribute cities into the following four categories: 1. Struggling Cities: These cities have a low GDP per capita today (i.e., GDP per capita less than $10,000), and a low ratio of projected growth in GDP per capita to projected growth in population between 2015 and 2030 (i.e., ratio less than 1), as compared to other cities. They are classified as struggling cities because, in the near future, they are likely to experience more rapid population growth than per capita economic growth, pointing to an impending resource gap. While this category includes predominantly sub-Saharan African cities, some cities in the Middle East and North Africa, and a few cities in South Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean are also represented. 2. Emerging Cities: These cities have a low GDP per capita today, and a high ratio of projected growth in GDP per capita to projected growth in population between 2015 and 2030, as compared to other cities. They are classified as emerging cities because, while their economic strength is low today, their projected economic growth is greater than their projected population growth, indicating projected increases in economic productivity. These cities are more likely to have the capacity to overcome current resource constraints and strengthen their position globally. Most of the cities in this category are in East Asia and the Pacific and South Asia, with some in Europe and Central Asia, and Latin America and the Caribbean as well. 3. Thriving Cities: These cities have a high GDP per capita today, and a high ratio of projected growth in GDP per capita to projected growth in population between 2015 and 2030, as compared to other cities. They are classified as thriving cities because, not only are they economically strong today, their economic growth is projected to outpace their urban population growth in coming years. These cities are growing and thriving. Cities from East Asia, Europe and Central Asia, North America, and Latin America and the Caribbean fall within this category. 4. Stabilizing Cities: These cities have a high GDP per capita today, and a low ratio of projected growth in GDP per capita to projected growth in population between 2015 and 2030, as compared to other cities. They are classified as stabilizing cities because they are economically strong today, but their economic growth is expected to be lower relative to their population growth when compared to emerging or thriving cities. In that sense, these cities are starting to stabilize and in some cases, their economies are starting to shrink. It is primarily cities from North America, Latin America, and the Middle East that fall within this category. In addition, WRI calculated the percent of projected population change for the same cities from the years 2015 to 2030. This data was taken from the same data providers. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: Climate and land-use change are major components of global environmental change. The first version of the Integrated Climate and Land Use Scenarios (ICLUS) project modeled population, residential development, and impervious surface cover changes by decade to the year 2100. Those modeling choices and assumptions were intended to be consistent with four scenarios from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). ICLUS version 2 is designed to be consistent with a more recent IPCC scenarios framework, drawing from two Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) and two Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). Improvements include the use of updated input data, integration of changing climate variables within the migration model, inclusion transportation network capacity and increase over time, growth in commercial and industrial land uses, and the use of population density-driven demands for residential housing, as well as commercial and industrial development. ICLUS v2.1 consists of population and land use projections produced specifically to support the Fourth National Climate Assessment. The methodology used to produce these population projections differs from ICLUS v2.0. The demographic components of change (i.e., rates of fertility and mortality) for ICLUS v2.1 were taken directly from the Wittgenstein Centre Data Explorer (http://witt.null2.net/shiny/wic/). These projections were produced much more recently than the Census projections used in ICLUS v2.0, and incorporate more recent observations of population change. SSP2 is a “middle-of-the-road” projection, where social, economic and technological trends do not shift markedly from historical patterns, resulting in a U.S. population of 455 million people by 2100. Domestic migration trends remain consistent with the recent past. The SSP5 narrative describes a rapidly growing and flourishing global economy that remains heavily dependent on fossil fuels, and a U.S. population that exceeds 730 million by 2100. ICLUS v2.1 land use projections under SSP5 result in a considerably larger expansion of developed lands relative to SSP2. Note that some versions of ICLUS projections do not include climate change projections to dynamically update location-specific amenities when calculating migration. These projections will include the “nocc” label in the file name to indicate this difference. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. title: Crop Land Area, Yield and Production - India
description: Crop Land Area, Yield and Production - India SOURCE: Directorate of Economics and Statistics, Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India LINK: https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web; https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf Overview The dataset comprises five-year averages of production (in tonnes), productivity/yield (in tonnes per hectare), and area (in hectares) for 55 major crops across India from 1997–98 to 2022–23. The information is provided at the district level, covering major seasonal time periods of each crop within each year. The yearly datasets were derived from crop-wise APY dataset (https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web). Methodology Pre-Processing: The dataset available as excel report was processed and joined with district shapefile (recent by mid of year 2022, containing 755 districts) obtained from Survey of India website. To simplify the presentation, the raw yearly data was averaged into five-year intervals to highlight trends in crop production and acreage across each district. The periods were labelled as follows: 1995-2000 as 2000, 2001-2005 as 2005, 2006-2010 as 2010, 2011-2015 as 2015, 2016-2020 as 2020, and 2021-2023 as 2023. This approach was adopted based on feedback from stakeholder engagements. Layers of interest: Rice Area (in Hectares), Rice Production (in Tonnes), Rice Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare), Cotton Area (in Hectares), Cotton Production (in Tonnes), Cotton Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare) Seasons considered for Rice crop: Kharif, Rabi, Autumn, Summer Seasons considered for Cotton crop: Kharif, Rabi The agricultural crop year in India runs from July to June. The cropping season is divided into two main seasons: (i) Kharif and (ii) Rabi, based on the monsoon. The Kharif season occurs from June/July to September/October during the southwest monsoon. It aligns with the Asian summer monsoon and is mostly rainfed, with limited irrigation arrangements. The Rabi season lasts from October to March and is grown under irrigated conditions. The Summer and Autumn seasons are shorter and found only in a few states. The Summer season runs from February/March to April/May and is mostly grown under irrigated conditions. The Autumn season, from May/June to October, is mainly for long-duration crops like sugarcane and some vegetable crops. For rice crop, the season is followed in particular states of India that do not receive considerable rains from the Asian summer monsoon. Area, Yield, and Production Estimation Methods The methods for estimating area, yield, and production of crops follow standardized processes under India's agricultural statistical framework. 1. Area Estimation Methods 1.1. Temporarily Settled States (Land Record States) Crop area is estimated through field-to-field enumeration by a village accountant (Patwari/Karnam). The data is recorded in the Khasra register (a field-wise crop record). The area statistics are aggregated at village, tehsil, district, and state levels. 1.2. Permanently Settled States (Non-Land Record States) Establishment of Agency for Reporting Agricultural Statistics (EARAS) is used: - A random sample of at least 20% of villages is surveyed annually. - Complete enumeration is conducted within selected villages. - The process ensures coverage of all villages over five years. 1.3. Non-Reporting Areas Area estimates are derived using remote sensing technology and aerial photography. Ground truthing and validation methods are used to improve accuracy. 2. Yield Estimation Methods General Crop Estimation Surveys (GCES) The yield is estimated through scientifically designed crop-cutting experiments (CCE). The methodology is as follows: 2.1. Sampling Design Stratified Multistage Random Sampling: - Strata: Administrative divisions (tehsil/block). - Primary Sampling Units: Villages (selected randomly). - Second-Stage Sampling Units: Fields within selected villages. - Ultimate Sampling Units: Experimental plots of standard size (e.g., 5m x 5m). 2.2. Plot Selection Two fields are randomly selected per village. A random plot (e.g., 5m x 5m) is located within each field using random numbers. For row-planted crops (like cotton), longer plots (e.g., 10m x 5m) are used. 2.3. Harvesting and Recording The experimental plot is harvested before the rest of the field. The produce is: - Weighed immediately for gross yield. - Adjusted if required (e.g., driage experiments for rice). 2.4. Driage Adjustments - Rice: Driage experiments are conducted to adjust for moisture content, ensuring yields are reported as dried grain weight. - Cotton: In the case of cotton, the final produce is expressed in terms of lint after adopting ginning percentage (kapas to lint) as obtained from the ginning factories. 3. Production Estimation Methods Area and yield are multiplied to estimate production at village, district, state, and national levels. 4. Validation of the Area, Production and Yield estimates Final aggregation and validation occur at the national level by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES). Production estimates are validated using: - Remote sensing data, - Historical trends, - Market and trade data, - Reports from local agricultural officers. For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf. Visualizing the Data The data is available as district-level aggregates. By selecting a specific crop, area, production, yield statistic, and preferred season, the relevant layer is displayed with a gradient based on the 2023 crop year, ranging from yellow (for low values) to green (with darker shades representing higher values). The cursor can be dragged over districts and clicked to view the 5-yearly averaged values from 1995 to 2023. The 'No Data' value, represented by black, indicates either that the season was not practiced in the district during that year or that data is unavailable from the source. title: Land Use Harmonization Projected Land Use under RCP 8.5 SSP5 (from REMIND-MAGPIE)
description: As part of the World Climate Research Program Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6), the international community is developing the next generation of advanced Earth System Models (ESM) able to estimate the combined effects of human activities (e.g. land use and fossil fuel emissions) on the carbon-climate system. In addition, a set of historical data based on HYDE, and multiple alternative scenarios of the future (2015-2100) developed by Integrated Assessment Model (IAM) teams, are being developed as input for these models. The goal of the Land-Use Harmonization (LUH2) project is to prepare a harmonized set of land-use scenarios that smoothly connects the historical reconstructions of land-use with the future projections in the format required for ESMs. The land-use harmonization strategy estimates the global fractional land-use patterns, underlying land-use transitions, and key agricultural management information, annually for the time period 850-2100 at 0.25° x 0.25° resolution, while minimizing the differences at the transition between the historical reconstruction ending conditions and IAM initial conditions, and working to preserve changes depicted by the IAMs in the future. Please see publications for more detail on the development of the Land-Use Harmonization model. In this data set Resource Watch displays the land-use patterns of the projected section of data (2015 – 2100) under RCP 8.5 SSP5 (from REMIND-MAGPIE), and classified pixels as the land use category that had the maximum fractional cover. RCP8.5 is an emissions pathway which reaches a radiative forcing of 8.5 W/m^2 and rising in 2100.

title: Wind Speed Potential
description: The Global Wind Atlas (GWA) mean wind speed dataset was generated by the Department of Wind Energy at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), World Bank Group and Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP). Mean wind speed is one of the key performance indicators of wind energy production. GWA starts with low resolution wind speed data and converts it to high resolution data using a downscaling process. The result of this process is a model of local wind climates over the globe (except the North and South Poles and far offshore ocean areas) at 1 kilometer resolution for three heights: 50 meters, 100 meters and 200 meters. title: Gridded Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
description: Global Gridded Geographically Based Economic Data (G-Econ), Version 4, provides a measure of global cell product (GCP): estimates for the amount of gross domestic product (GDP) produced in each grid cell of a 1-degree grid of the world using 2 metrics: GCP measured in the market exchange rate (MER) from local currencies into US$, and GCP measured in purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts country currency GCP according to the equivalent amount of US$ needed to purchase a standardized collection of goods in the country using the country's currency. GCP is defined as the gross value added by activities in a grid cell. Gross value is calculated as the total value of the outputs of local businesses providing goods and services in the grid cell, minus the value of inputs bought by those businesses. The data and methods used to calculate local added value are different for different countries, as the data available are different for different countries. State- and county level gross value data are used whenever possible. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

title: Gray Water Footprint and Pollution Levels
description: The Twente Water Centre at the University of Twente (TWC) created a global assessment of nitrogen-related water pollution in river basins, with the option to specify the pollution source by economic sector, and by crop for the agricultural sector. Anthropogenic nitrogen (N) loads to freshwater are estimated to calculate the resultant gray water footprints (GWFs), and relate the GWFs per river basin to runoff to calculate the N-related water pollution level (WPL) per catchment. These calculations were created at a 5-by-5 arc minute spatial resolution over the period 2002-2010. The GWF is calculated by dividing the N load by the difference between the ambient water quality standard for N (the maximum acceptable concentration) and the natural concentration of N in the receiving water body. The water pollution level (WPL), which measures the degree of pollution within a catchment, is estimated as the ratio of the total of GWF in a catchment to the actual runoff from that catchment. The artificial fertilizer application rate data came primarily from the International Fertilizer Industry Association (IFA) and was supplemented with data from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Frost Free Season
description: Frost free season represents the annual average longest streak of days above freezing, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](01ae2fd7-b818-429f-a27e-a36c8def971a) as a replacement.**_ The Yield Gap and Potential Yield for Major Crops data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use (UMN IonE), and the Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC) for 16 major crops. Yield gaps are defined as the difference between observed crop yields and the potential yield at the same location. Yield gaps were estimated by comparing observed yields to potential yields determined by identifying high-yielding areas within zones, or bins, of similar climate. To classify climates, 2 parameters, which are known to be fundamental drivers of plant growth, were used to describe a region's climate: growing degree days (GDD) and a crop soil moisture index (the ratio of actual evapotranspiration to potential evapotranspiration). For each climate zone and each crop, a table was generated containing the yield, harvest area, and latitude/longitude position information for each grid cell included in the distribution. The data were sorted from the grid cells by their yield values, ranking them from lowest to highest yield. The grid cells' respective harvest areas were then accumulated until arriving at the statistical information of interest: the mean, median, and 90th percentile yields. The percentage of a crop's harvested area was calculated to define a percentile yield value. The data draw on average of census data between 1997 and 2003 and are shown as 2000 at a 5 minute x 5 minute spatial resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Hydropolitical Tension and Institutional Vulnerability
description: ### Overview The Transboundary Freshwater Dispute Database (TFDD) catalogs the number and delineation of the world's international river basins and also contains physical, socioeconomic, and political data relating to each of them. In the context of these datasets, an international river basin is defined by its ultimate outlet to an ocean, sea, or inland water body and has year-round flow crossing or drawing a political border. This database includes data at the scale of basins as well as basin country units, which is an area of an international river basin that falls within a particular country. The Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension estimates the relative level of risk a basin or basin country unit has for political tension over its transboundary rivers. This risk is based on: 1. **water infrastructure development**: the ability to deal with disputes arising from the development of new water infrastructure 2. **institutional vulnerability**: the capacity of a basin country unit to absorb tension, which is expressed by the presence or absence of treaties, treaty provisions, and river basin organizations This data was calculated by TFDD-affiliated researchers as a part of the Governance thematic group within the Transboundary Water Assessment Programme's River Basin Component. ### Methodology The delineation and count of international river basins and basin country units were determined using the [Register of International River Basins](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/content/register-international-river-basins) and watershed boundaries from the [HydroBASINs](https://www.hydrosheds.org/page/hydrobasins) dataset. HydroBASINS provides global coverage of watershed boundaries with several levels of sub-basin delineations, including watersheds that range in scale from tens to millions of square kilometers (see [Lehner & Gill, 2013](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.9740)). For full documentation on the spatial boundary data, please see the [methodology](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07900627.2019.1572497). Institutional Vulnerability is measured by five components of formal transboundary cooperation. The five components are: 1. at least one water treaty 2. at least one treaty with an allocation mechanism 3. at least one treaty with a flow variability management mechanism 4. at least one treaty with a conflict resolution mechanism 5. at least one river basin organization The presence of a component is summed to give the institutional vulnerability score from 0 to 5, with 0 being the most vulnerable and 5 being the least vulnerable. Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension is calculated based on the basin country unit's institutional vulnerability score and the presence of a large dam or water diversion project in the basin country unit or upstream of it. If a basin country unit has a lower score for its institutional vulnerability and has infrastructure development in the basin country unit or upstream, it is in a higher risk category for Hydropolitical tension. Relative Risk ranges from 1 (very low risk) to 5 (very high risk). For full documentation on the metrics shown in this dataset, please see the [Transboundary River Basins report](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/sites/transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/files/Database/ResearchProjects/TWAP/GEF_TWAPRB_FullTechnicalReport_compressed.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset.
