title: Aqueduct Baseline Water Depletion
description: ### Overview Baseline water depletion measures the ratio of total water consumption to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. A higher ratio indicates larger impact on the local water supply and decreased water availability for downstream users. These ratios were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low water stress (<5%) to extremely high water stress (>75%). Total water consumption includes domestic, industrial, irrigation and livestock consumptive uses. Available renewable water supplies include the impact of upstream water use and large dams on downstream water availability. Water depletion values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). Baseline water depletion is similar to baseline water stress; however, instead of looking at total water withdrawal (i.e. all water removed from source), baseline water depletion is calculated using consumptive withdrawal only (i.e. water withdrawn but not returned to source). ### Methodology Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB 2), to calculate five indicators. Baseline water depletion is one of those indicators and was calculated using the gross and net total consumption and available water per sub-basin time series from the default PCR-GLOBWB 2 run. The model was first used to calculate a time series of water depletion per catchment per month. To calculate water depletion, total water consumptions were divided by the available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Net consumptive water use was subtracted from the total available renewable water supply before the ratio was calculated. This results in 12 monthly time series of water depletion per sub-basin. Water resources in delta sub-basins were pooled. Next, the time series were converted into baseline values using an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. For example, the regression output for January 2019 represents the chronic, long-term condition of water depletion in January’s from 1979 to 2019. This was repeated for every month, and then averaged into an annual value. All raw values were limited to a maximum of 100% and a minimum of 0%. Sub-basins that were classified “Arid and low water use” were handled separately and were given a raw value for baseline water depletion of -1. Finally, raw baseline water depletion values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw baseline water depletion values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 5% - Low to medium (1-2): 5 - 25% - Medium to high (2-3): 25 - 50% - High (3-4): 50 - 75% - Extremely high (4-5): > 75% - Arid and low water use: -1 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

Percentage of Energy Consumption from Renewable Sources
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the percentage of total final energy consumption(TFEC) that comes from renewable sources in 259 countries from 1990 to present. In this dataset, renewable energy sources are defined as hydropower, solid and liquid biofuels, wind, solar, biogas, geothermal, marine, and waste to energy. The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative, and the data was compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations Statistics Divisions (UNSD). IEA and UNDC are the primary developers of internationally comparable national energy statistics. This dataset tracks the progress of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 7.2, to advance the target of increase substantially the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) data from the SE4ALL Database. ### Methodology This dataset was compiled using data from IEA and UNSD. Renewable energy consumption was divided by total final energy consumption to calculate the share of renewable energy in the total final energy consumption of each country. Renewable energy consumption was defined as the final consumption of renewables plus the amount of electricity and heat consumption estimated to have come from renewable energy sources. Total final energy consumption was defined as the sum of the final energy consumption in the transport, industry, residential, services, and other sectors. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.seforall.org/sites/default/files/l/2013/09/9-gtf_ch4.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) data from the SE4ALL Database. Actual and Potential Crop Yields
description: Global Yield Gap Atlas Crop Yield Gap (GYGA-Yg) data compare the performance of crop yields in a location to the theoretically potential yields with no water stress (Yp) and potential yields in presence of some water stress (Yw). Yp and Yw are determined by the biophysical characteristics of the location and the needs of each crop type. This information can be used to identify high- and low-performing crop-growing regions, and to motivate technology and expertise transfer to address suboptimal yields. GYGA-Yg data provide a new perspective in the field of crop yield gap analysis, as they move beyond using gridded climate data to incorporate locally observed climate and production data as much as possible. The smallest unit of analysis for the GYGA-Yg is the region around a reference weather station (RWS). Each RWS is surrounded by a 100-km radius circular buffer. These buffers are then intersected with GYGA climate zones (GYGA-CZs), soil types, and cropping system information. These factors are used as inputs to a crop model to estimate Yw and/or Yp for each RWS buffer zone. GYGA-CZs are defined by growing degree days (GDDs), temperature seasonality, and an annual aridity index (AI), all of which are measured on a 5 arc minute grid. GDDs are defined as the number of days that the mean temperature is above 0°C. Temperature seasonality is calculated to be the standard deviation of the 12 mean monthly temperatures. AI is the ratio of mean annual precipitation over mean annual evapotranspiration. Cropping system information includes the amount of harvested area, the cropping intensity of growth, and aspects of management such as use of irrigation, planting date, and development timeline of various crops. Yield gaps are calculated as the difference between Yw/Yp (simulated yield potential with and without water stress, respectively) and on-farm yields (Ya). Ya are taken from recent national crop-specific yield statistics at the finest resolution available. Ideally, this is at a scale smaller than the GYGA-CZ clipped RWS buffer areas. If national statistics are not available, household surveys that ask about crop production may be used, such as are collected by groups like the World Bank and the Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research (CGIAR). If these are not available, then GYGA country agronomist experts' estimates are used. If there are insufficiently detailed estimates available from country experts, the last resort is to use country-level production statistics.

title: Daily Imagery
description: ### Overview The Daily Imagery dataset shows near real-time global satellite imagery from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument on board the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (SNPP) satellite. SNPP passes over each pole 14 times per day and crosses the equator at 01:30 local time. VIIRS contains a radiometer that creates imagery by collecting wavelengths of light in the visible bands of the electromagnetic spectrum. The imagery created is at a spatial resolution of 250 meters (m) and has been updated daily since 2015. The Daily Imagery dataset can be used for fire and air quality monitoring, along with flood and sea ice mapping. In addition, long-term records of global daily imagery data can contribute to scientists’ understanding of climate change, earth’s atmosphere, natural disasters and weather predictions. The SNPP satellite is a joint mission from the North American Space Administration (NASA) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (NOAA). It serves as an improvement to the previously launched Earth Observing System (EOS) Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and is part of the future [Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)](https://www.jpss.noaa.gov/mission_and_instruments.html). ### Methodology The Daily Imagery dataset was created with data collected by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument on board the joint NASA/NOAA SNPP satellite. The SNPP satellite passes above or nearly above both poles on each revolution. For this dataset VIIRS collected imagery in the “true color” spectral band, which is a combination of wavelengths similar to what the human eye would see. The bands of light collected were in the VIIRS I and M bands. The I band utilizes a high-resolution 375 m sensor that collects red light, while the M band utilizes a moderate-resolution 750 m sensor that collects blue and green light. After the spectral band data was collected it was compiled to create a 250 m RGB (Red, Green, Blue) composite image of the earth. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows the [Nighttime Imagery] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cli061nrt-Daily-Nighttime-lights) dataset from the VIIRS instrument on board the SNPP satellite. Peatlands
description: ### Overview This dataset includes the most-updated effort to map the global distribution of peatlands. [Peatlands are unique and underappreciated ecosystems, rich in both carbon and biological diversity](https://www.wri.org/blog/2018/01/save-indonesias-carbon-rich-peatlands-start-mapping-them). Peat forms when dead plants partially decay in water-saturated soils and organic matter gradually accumulates, layer upon layer, over hundreds or even thousands of years. Peatlands are important because they store soil carbon and provide water resources and habitats for a range of rare, threatened, or declining species. This dataset estimates the global peatland area to be 4.23 million square kilometers, almost 3% of the world's land area. This dataset was published in 2017 by researchers at the University of Leeds. It may provide a useful reference for policymakers and researchers interested in global ecosystem biodiversity, climate change, carbon cycles, and water resources. It may also help provide support for wetland protection and restoration. ### Methodology The global dataset is put together by compiling the most high quality and freely available data from a wide range of sources that describe peatland distributions at global, regional, and national levels. Data includes information derived from digitized soil maps, wetland databases, and satellite imagery. For areas in Hokkaido (Japan), Mongolia, and North Korea, where peatland-specific datasets were not available, the authors estimated peatland extent based on the distribution of histosols derived from the Harmonized World Soil Database v1.2 (HWSD). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0341816217303004?via%3Dihub). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. We recommend using [this dataset](fc6dea95-37a6-41a0-8c99-38b7a2ea7301) as a replacement.**_ The Human Development Index (HDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, a sufficient education, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The HDI is calculated for 188 countries annually. title: Urban Expansion Probabilities
description: ### Overview This dataset shows global forecasts of probabilities for urban expansion through 2050. It separates the data into five shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs), at a 5 kilometer (km) resolution. SSPs represent how different policy and societal choices will affect greenhouse gas emissions. The five scenarios used in this analysis are labeled as: - SSP1: Sustainability – Taking the Green Road (low challenges to mitigation and adaptation) - SSP2: Middle of the Road (medium challenges to mitigation and adaptation) - SSP3: Regional Rivalry – A Rocky Road (high challenges to mitigation and adaptation) - SSP4: Inequality – A Road Divided (low challenges to mitigation, high challenges to adaptation) - SSP5: Fossil-fueled Development – Taking the Highway (high challenges to mitigation, low challenges to adaptation) The dataset was created with information from a combination of five sources based on current urban land extent, population rates, Gross Domestic Product (GDP) information, and SSP scenarios. It is important to understand urban expansion because it can cause implications for warming, water scarcity, land use, and other environmental and social challenges. This dataset can be combined with other socioeconomic data to further examine the impacts of urban expansion. For instance, the dataset authors predicted urban expansion-induced warning in cities and suggested that it will increase extreme heat risks for about half of the future urban population. This will primarily affect communities in the tropical Global South that lack the adaptive capacity to meet environmental change. Policymakers can use this dataset to restrict or redistribute urban expansion and design strategies needed to mitigate Urban Heat Islands (UHIs) to reduce their negative impacts on human health, urban ecosystems, energy systems, and infrastructure. This dataset was published by Seto Lab, based at Yale School of the Environment. ### Methodology Researchers created this dataset using the URBANMOD-ZIPE model. The URBANMOD-ZIPE model was based on a 2012 global urban land change model, URBANMOD, and used to forecast pixels of urban expansion probabilities. The input data sources used for the updated model were: 1. urban land extent from the Global Human Settlement grid 2. urban population from the United Nations 3. Gross Domestic Product from the World Bank 4. future scenarios of the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) from the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis There were two phases to the model. Phase 1 predicted the quantities of urban land by 2050. This was done using a fixed effect panel regression model to relate urban land per capita to GDP per capita. Phase 2 utilized a land change model to allocate new urban lands to map pixels using slope, distance to roads, population density, and land covers as the drivers of land change. The final dataset was produced in raster format at a spatial resolution of 5 km. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/ab4b71). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. Resource Watch has previously shown this data for urban expansion probabilities for 2030. This dataset was archived because the methodology has been changed and the global forecasts of probabilities for urban expansion through 2050 is now available. You can still access the archived data [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit005-Urban-Expansion-Probabilities_replacement). ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: [Archived] Maritime Boundaries
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](6af67024-b917-4944-851a-152b566ff1a8) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Maritime Boundaries dataset shows boundaries for exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas (TS) and contiguous zones (CZ) for coastal countries around the world. The [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)](http://www.vliz.be/en/imis?module=ref&refid=325469) defined the EEZ, CZ and TS maritime boundaries and coastal baselines. An EEZ is a sea zone over which a country has special rights to explore and use marine resources. Typically, a country’s EEZ extends 200 nautical miles (NM) from its coast (or baseline), unless that distance would overlap with another country’s EEZ. TS are coastal waters that are the sovereign territory of a given country. This zone extends a maximum of 12 NM from a country’s baseline. A CZ is a sea zone that extends an additional 12 NM beyond the outer edge of the TS (up to 24 NM from a country’s baseline). Countries have limited legal rights within the CZ. Data for the Maritime Boundaries dataset was published by the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in 2018 and is available for download from [Marine Regions](https://marineregions.org/). The Maritime Boundaries dataset is a useful tool for managing and displaying marine data. It provides a standardized map of global maritime boundaries. The Maritime Boundaries dataset is useful for linking marine information, such as species distribution lists or coral reef health, to particular countries. The dataset also shows the various jurisdictional reaches of countries. This is important for understanding marine resource management and the rights that countries have to protect their waters. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was generated by the [Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ)](https://www.vliz.be/en), a non-profit organization dedicated to scientific research on the ocean, seas, coasts and tidal estuaries. Based in Belgium VLIZ was established in 1999 by the Flemish government and [the Research Foundation - Flanders](https://www.fwo.be/en/). The central focus of VLIZ is to provide knowledge to the research community, educators, the general public, policymakers and marine industries. ### Methodology The boundaries shown in the Maritime Boundaries dataset were generated from a combination of **normal**, **straight** and **archipelagic** baselines. The UNCLOS defines a **normal** baseline as the low-water line along a country’s coast. A **straight** baseline is a straight line representing the baseline where there is a fringe of islands along the coast, or the coast is heavily indented. **Archipelagic** baselines apply to archipelago countries, which are made of a group of islands. These baselines are straight lines that connect the coastlines and contain the main islands of the country. Normal baselines were drawn using a combination of the [Esri Countries 2014 dataset](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=ac80670eb213440ea5899bbf92a04998) and the [United Nations Environmental Program (UNEP) Coral Reef Distribution dataset](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/1), referred to as the World Countries 2014 dataset. Coral reef data was used to draw baselines for countries where reefs were a fundamental part of their maritime boundaries. Straight and archipelagic baselines were drawn based on [definitions from the UN](https://www.un.org/Depts/los/LEGISLATIONANDTREATIES/regionslist.htm) or maritime treaties and agreements. Countries typically define borders at sea in agreements with their neighbors. These borders were used when available. Median lines were drawn between countries where borders at sea were not specified. Median lines connect points at equal distance from neighboring coastal countries. The baselines were used to generate boundaries of EEZ, TS and CZ sea zones. The boundaries are seaward distances of 200 EEZ, 12 TS and 24 CZ NM from a country’s baseline. Polygons representing the EEZ, TS and CZ areas were calculated using a buffer distance measured from the combination of straight, archipelagic and normal baselines. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was created by merging the EEZ, TS and CZ boundaries with the World Countries 2014 dataset using the [Pairwise Dissolve tool](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/tool-reference/analysis/pairwise-dissolve.htm) in ESRI ArcGIS Pro 2.5.0. Landlocked countries were removed before merging and added in afterward. Differences between coastlines in the EEZ and World Countries 2014 datasets caused small gaps in the polygons. These gaps were fixed in QGis 3.0 using the [Delete Holes tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectorgeometry.html#delete-holes) and the [Difference tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectoroverlay.html#difference). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.marineregions.org/eezmethodology.php). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. VLIZ also provides boundaries of internal waters, archipelagic waters and high seas. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

[Archived] Ramsar Internationally Important Wetlands
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](2ac1f43c-30bc-4ed9-846c-8443ce4987a9) as a replacement.**_ Ramsar wetlands refer to "internally important" wetlands as defined by the Convention on Wetlands and are designated by each contracting party. At the time of joining the Convention, each contracting party must designate at least one wetland site within their territory for inclusion in the List of Wetlands of International Importance (the Ramsar List). These Ramsar sites acquire a new national and international status. They are recognized as being of significant value not only for the country or the countries in which they are located but for humanity as a whole. There are currently over 2,200 Ramsar sites around the world. They cover over 2.1 million km2, an area larger than Mexico. Parties continue to designate wetlands for inclusion on the list. They select suitable wetlands for designation by referring to the criteria for identifying wetlands of international importance. The Convention has provided guidance to contracting parties on the management of Ramsar sites, in addition to its guidance on the wise use of all wetlands. The inclusion of a wetland on the list signifies the government’s commitment to take the steps necessary to ensure that the site’s ecological character is maintained. The Convention includes various measures to respond to threats to the ecological character of sites. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average minimum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the minimum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average minimum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in annual average minimum temperature is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average minimum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily minimum temperature data over a given year. The average annual minimum temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average minimum temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual minimum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Biodiversity Hotspots
description: First defined in 1988 by scientist Norman Myers, biodiversity hotspots are areas characterized by high levels of endemic plants coupled with significant habitat loss. Specifically, a region must meet the following criteria to achieve the hotspot classification formulated by Conservation International (CI): (1) at least 1,500 species of vascular plants (>0.5% of the world’s total) are endemic; and (2) at least 70% of the original natural vegetation has been lost. When Myers first defined the term, he identified 10 tropical forest hotspots. The need to pinpoint priority conservation regions led CI to adopt the term and reassess the hotspot concept. In this process, CI introduced quantitative thresholds (see above) and added additional regions. At that time, there were 25 hotspots. Because of the constant change in environmental threats and the improved understanding of biodiversity, CI has since revisited the hotspots to refine boundaries, update information, and add new regions to create this global data set. This process produced an additional 10 hotspots, bringing the total to 35. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. title: Standard Precipitation Index
description: ### Overview The dataset shown on Resource Watch shows global precipitation rates for 2006 to 2019. It utilizes the Standard Precipitation Index (SPI) as a form of measurement, which shows how precipitation during a time period varies to historical averages for the region. SPI is based on how many standard deviations the precipitation value is away from the mean value. The dataset was created using the Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Stations (CHIRPS) model, which analyzes average monthly historical precipitation rates, satellite imagery, and local weather stations to create new data points that are released every 5 days. The final dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.05 degrees (around 5 kilometers at the equator). This dataset was created in collaboration between the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) Earth Resources Observation and Science Center and University of California, Santa Barbara Climate Hazards Group. It was created to help understand how precipitation varies in space and time to assist in predicting droughts. Additionally, it helps put seasonal drought conditions in perspective with historical conditions to provide governments with an understanding of their severity. An early warning system and understanding of seasonal variation are integral for governments creating water use and sustainability policies. ### Methodology The final Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Stations (CHIRPS) dataset was created in three parts. First researchers created the Climate Hazards Precipitation Climatology (CHPClim) dataset for historical monthly precipitation from 1980-2009. The CHPClim dataset was formed with a combination of satellite observations, data from weather stations, and rainfall predictors, like elevation, latitude, and longitude. Second, to create near-present rainfall data researchers reviewed satellite imagery to determine how long cold cloud tops (<235° K) were present in an area. Cold cloud tops are representative of rain. This information was used to estimate rainfall for the region in millimeters over a 5 day period and mapped using a grid system. The historical averages from CHPClim were compared with near-present rainfall estimates to determine how the rainfall compares to historical rates and help produce an unbiased estimate. Lastly, observations were taken from the five closest weather stations for each 0.05 degree grid cell. Values from each weather station were weighted based on their proximity to the grid cell. The results were presented using the Standard Precipitation Index (SPI). SPI is a way to compare recent precipitation to historical averages for a region. It is based on the number of standard deviations rainfall is away from the historical values. In this case, standard deviation is used to express how far recent precipitation data is from historical mean precipitation rates compared to all of the prior rainfall data for the area. For example, if a region had fairly constant precipitation rates it can have a higher standard deviation with a smaller difference in precipitation compared to a region with a lot of variability. In the final dataset the number of standard deviations (SD) away from historical mean precipitation rates were given descriptive titles as follows: - SPI ≤ -2 SD = Extremely Dry; - -2 SD < SPI ≤ -1.5 SD = Severely Dry; - -1.5 SD < SPI ≤ -1 SD = Moderately Dry; - -1 SD < SPI ≤ 1 SD = Near Normal; - 1 SD < SPI ≤ 1.5 SD = Moderately Wet; - 1.5 SD < SPI ≤ 2 SD = Severely Wet, - SPI ≥ 2 SD = Extremely Wet. The dataset was created by Climate Hazards Group at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Satellite imagery used to determine precipitation and cloud cover are thermal infrared (IR) satellite observations from two NOAA sources, the Climate Prediction Center (CPC) IR and the National Climatic Data Center (NCDC) B1 IR, the Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM) 3B42 product from NASA, and atmospheric model rainfall fields from the NOAA Climate Forecast System, version 2 (CFSv2). Weather station data was collected from the Agromet Group of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) and the Global Historical Climate Network (GHCN). The final results were mapped globally between the latitudes of 50°S–50°N and longitudes 180°E–180°W at a spatial resolution of 0.05 degrees (around 5 km). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for every year between 1980 to present are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_023_standard_precipitation_index). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

Vegetation Health Index
description: The STAR Vegetation Health Index is a product from NOAA's National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NOAA-NESDIS) Global and Regional Vegetation Heath (VH) system estimating vegetation health, moisture condition, and thermal condition. VH products can be used as proxy data for monitoring vegetation health, drought, soil saturation, moisture and thermal conditions, fire risk, greenness of vegetation cover, vegetation fraction, leaf area index, start/end of the growing season, crop and pasture productivity, teleconnection with ENSO, desertification, mosquito-borne diseases, invasive species, ecological resources, land degradation, etc. The VH indices range from 0 to 100 characterizing changes in vegetation conditions from extremely poor (0) to excellent (100). Fair conditions are coded by green color (50), which changes to brown and red when conditions deteriorate and to blue when they improve. The VH reflects indirectly a combination of chlorophyll and moisture content in the vegetationhealth and also changes in thermal conditions at the surface.Monitoring vegetation health (condition), including drought detection and watch, is based on radiance measurements in the visible (VIS), near infrared (NIR), and 10.3-11.3 micrometers thermal (T) bands (channels) of the Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR). These measurements are processed to reduce long-term noise. The VIS and NIR values were converted to the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI=(NIR-VIS)/(NIR+VIS)) and the T to brightness temperature (BT) using a look-up table. The NDVI and BT were filtered in order to eliminate high frequency noise. They were also adjusted for a non-uniformity of the land surface due to climate and ecosystem differences using multi-year NDVI and BT data. The NDVI and BT were converted to the Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), Temperature Condition Index (TCI), and Vegetation Health Index (VHI).The Vegetation Health Index (VHI) is a proxy characterizing vegetation health or a combined estimation of moisture and thermal conditions. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Global Inventory of Solar Energy Installations
description: ### Overview This is the first global inventory of commercial, industrial and utility scale solar energy stations. It has located nearly 70,000 facilities around the world, and has enriched this data with facility installation dates, previous land use, and proximity to conservation and indigenous protected areas. This dataset covers solar energy stations between June 2016 to October 2018. The solar installation location data is critical for improving the accuracy of current inventories and future forecasting, helping countries to align their energy systems to their net zero targets. When combined with weather data, the generating behaviour of precisely-located solar generating facilities becomes more predictable, allowing a larger share of total power generation to come from solar energy.The data will also help to ascertain the impact of solar installations on the natural and human-made world. The planet-scale study carried out by the team reveals some differences between top-down estimates of solar photovoltaic energy generating capacity reported by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the new bottom-up asset-level inventory. More generating capacity has been found in the United States (7,639 facilities, 54.1 GW), for example, than reported in top-down inventories (40.2GW), however the inventory for China (18,449 facilities,167.4 GW) almost precisely matches top-down estimates (173.5 GW). This dataset was developed by the University of Oxford, Descartes Lab, and the World Resources Institute (WRI). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [global power plants](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Powerwatch) from this research team. title: Connectivity of Container Ports
description: The Container Port Connectivity Index (CPCI) is constructed to represent the structure of the global container shipping network and combines concepts of economics and network topology to assign inbound- and outbound-connectivity scores to all ports in this network. A port with a high inbound score can be interpreted as being a good collection point for global goods, and a port with a high outbound score can be interpreted as being a good distribution point for global goods. The Container Port Connectivity Index measures the trade connectivity of ports within the network of container shipping and is broken down into an inbound and outbound index. The data on Resource Watch represent both the inbound and outbound indices of global container ports, calculated using container ship scheduled services for the month of September 2017. This index is the result of research performed at the Georgia Tech Panama Logistics Innovation and Research Center, Chulalongkorn University Department of Industrial Engineering, and University of Hull Logistics Institute. The CPCI is based on a network representation of container ports, where nodes in network represent individual ports and connections between nodes are weighted based on measures defined by the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) Liner Shipping Connectivity Index (LSCI). This study uses the same 5 statistics as the LSCI, but on a port-to-port scale instead of the country-world scale of the LSCI: the number of shipping liner services calling between 2 ports, the number of companies providing those services, the number of ships in those services, the combined container capacity of those ships, and the capacity of the largest ship in service. The Hyperlink-Induced-Topic-Search (HITS) algorithm is used to calculate the inbound- and outbound-connectivity of all ports in this network. Concepts of economics are captured by the LSCI measures included in the weights of the network, and network topology is captured by the application of the HITS algorithm to assign inbound- and outbound-connectivity scores. These scores are ordered to create the CPCI. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: International Water Event Database
description: The International Water Events Database is a searchable database documenting over 6,400 historical international water related events from 1948 to 2008. Events in the database concern water as a scarce or consumable resource or as a quantity to be managed. Event information includes the basins and countries involved, date occurred, affected area, Basin at Risk (BAR) scale (water event intensity scale) rating, and a detailed summary of the event. The BAR scale indicates the level of intensity of conflict or cooperation related to water events and ranks events from -7, representing a formal declaration of war due to the waste, to +7, representing a voluntary unification into one nation. This data set searches and categorizes existing political science data sets. The sources of this data set include the Data Development for International Research (DDIR) project, the International Crisis Behavior Project (ICB), the Conflict and Peace Data Bank (COPDAB), the Global Event Data System (GEDS), LEXIS-NEXIS, the Foreign Broadcast Information Service (FBIS), and the Freshwater Dispute Database Project (TFDD). Mining Concessions
description: ### Overview The Mining Concessions dataset shows locations of public land allocated by governments to companies for mineral extraction. The dataset is a compilation of concession data from Brazil, Cambodia, Cameroon, Canada, Colombia, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gabon, Mexico, Peru and Republic of the Congo. Information about the company, the mineral being extracted, concession status and concession area in hectares (ha) is included in the Mining Concessions dataset. Mining Concessions data is typically from government agencies, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), the public domain or nonprofits, although the data source and date vary by country. Mining activities can have a profound impact on the landscape and environment. Mining companies clear large areas of land and extract huge volumes of rock to build surface and underground mines. This can disrupt the local ecosystems and cause erosion and groundwater contamination. In addition to affecting landscapes, mining contributes to climate change by releasing greenhouse gases. A [study from the Sustainable Minerals Institute](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41561-020-0531-3) estimated that the mining industry was responsible for 10% of energy-related greenhouse gas emissions in 2018. Understanding where mining is permitted provides information about potential environmental impact and can help inform policy decisions about conservation efforts. The Mining Concessions dataset was generated by [Global Forest Watch (GFW)](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/about/), an organization established in 1997 by the [World Resources Institute](https://www.wri.org/). WRI is an independent, non-governmental global research organization which seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. They provide data and research about climate, energy, food, forests, water, cities and oceans. GFW uses satellite data and cloud computing to monitor deforestation in near real-time. Understanding when and where deforestation is occurring is critical for ending illegal deforestation, fires, and unsustainable practices. Farmers and landowners can use this data to protect their land and resources. Additionally, this data can be used by business owners and the public to monitor the environmental impacts of activities like logging, mining and farming. ### Methodology The Mining Concessions dataset was generated by compiling concession data from Brazil, Cambodia, Cameroon, Canada, Colombia, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Gabon, Mexico, Peru and Republic of the Congo. The term “concession” was used as a general descriptor for licenses, permits, or other contracts that give private companies the rights to extract minerals from public lands. Concession terminology varied by country and included mining permit, mineral permit, tenure and license. Most locations have additional information about each mining concession such as the company name, material being mined, status and area impacted (in hectares). GFW collected data from a variety of sources. The most common source was natural resources or mining-specific government agencies. Data from the public domain (company websites, news reports, NGOs) was used for countries where data was not available from government agencies. This data was used to create polygons representing the locations and boundaries of concessions. Additional information such as company name and concession status were added to the polygons as attributes. The Mining Concessions dataset was published in 2019, though the exact dates vary by country. Concession data for each country is available on the [GFW Open Data Portal](https://data.globalforestwatch.org/search?q=mining). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Projected Change in Frost Free Season U.S. (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Cumulative Precipitation
description: Annual average total precipitation, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

Access to an Improved Water Source (Urban)
description: ### Overview This dataset includes the percentage of people using drinking water from an improved source that is accessible, available when needed, and free from contamination. It provides values for the years 2000 to 2017 for urban populations. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), safely managed drinking water is defined as an improved water source that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from fecal and priority chemical contamination. Improved water sources include piped water, boreholes or tubewells, protected dug wells, protected springs, and packaged and delivered water. WHO and UNICEF’s Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene prepared this dataset. Access to safe drinking water is a human right, not a privilege, for everyone. Access to safe water can reduce illness and death from disease, improve health, reduce poverty, and lead to socioeconomic development. Yet many countries still lack access to safe drinking water. Children are especially vulnerable to deaths and illnesses related to lack of access to proper drinking water services. In addition, women and girls are almost two and a half times more likely than men and boys to fetch water, reducing their time for other activities, such as attending school. ### Methodology This dataset was developed based on administrative sources, national censuses, and nationally representative surveys. A weighted average is calculated to aggregate subnational data to the national level. There are three criteria for an improved water source: (1) accessibility: water should be accessible on the premises, (2) availability: water should be available when needed, and (3) quality: water supplied should be free from contamination. The WHO/UNICEF JMP provides national estimates only when data is available on drinking water quality and at least one of the criteria. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://databank.worldbank.org/reports.aspx?source=2&type=metadata&series=SH.H2O.SMDW.ZS). ### Additional Information Additional data for the percentage of the population with access to an improved water source at [rural](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat005c-Access-to-an-Improved-Water-Source-Rural) and [national](https://.resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat005a-Access-to-an-Improved-Water-Source-National-Level_1) levels are available on Resource Watch. title: Anthropogenic Biomes
description: ### Overview The Anthropogenic Biomes dataset illustrate human transformation and use of the terrestrial biosphere over the past 12,000 years at 73 time points between 10,000 BCE and 2015 CE. Anthromes (Anthropogenic Biomes) represent the globally significant patterns of Earth’s ecology created and sustained by human populations and their use of land, including urban, village, cropland, rangeland and semi-natural anthromes, together with wildlands without evidence of human populations or land use. Anthromes were mapped using gridded global estimates of human population density and land use from the History of the Global Environment database [(HYDE version 3.2)](https://doi.org/10.17026/dans-25g-gez3). The dataset has global coverage from 10,000 BC to 2015 AD at a resolution of 5 arc minutes (about 10 km). Much attention has focused on the role of recent global changes in human populations and their use of land in transforming climate, ecosystems, biodiversity, and the functioning of the Earth system as a whole, as part of a planetary transition to the Anthropocene. Yet humans have been transforming landscapes around the world for thousands of years, from hunter-gatherer burning to clear land, to the emergence and spread of agriculture, to the rise of large-scale urban industrial societies. To understand the causes and consequences of Earth’s transformation by human societies, the full, continuous trajectory of these anthropogenic transformations of the terrestrial biosphere must be examined from their first beginnings to the present day. As with prior anthrome datasets, the Anthropogenic Biomes dataset offers many opportunities to investigate the global consequences of long-term changes in the global reshaping of ecology by human societies.The many other assessments of Earth’s ecological and social patterns, processes, and dynamics that have utilized prior anthrome datasets are also clear targets for new and improved investigations using this dataset, including, for example, studies of biogeography and biodiversity, primary productivity, fire, conservation, disease and ecological research itself. The Anthropogenic Biomes dataset was developed by the [Anthroecology Lab](https://anthroecology.org/) working group, part of the Department of Geography & Environmental Systems at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County (UMBC). The Anthroecology Lab explores the ecology of populated landscapes at local, regional and global scales towards the goal of making ecosystem management more sustainable. ### Methodology The rule-based mapping approach of [Anthromes 2.0](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1466-8238.2010.00540.x) utilized 5 arc minute gridded global data for population density and percent cover by crops, pastures and urban areas from [HYDE 3.1](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1466-8238.2010.00587.x) together with global data for potential vegetation cover, irrigation and rice. To classify and map anthromes from 10,000 BCE to 2015 CE, the HYDE 3.2 dataset was used, as it now provides all necessary input data for anthromes classification over this entire interval in a standard open-access dataset. The Anthropogenic Biomes dataset covers all of Earth’s land surface with 20 anthrome classes,by including an anthrome class for uninhabited ice-covered land areas. These 20 detailed classes are grouped into six anthrome levels: Dense settlements, Villages, Croplands, Rangelands, Seminatural lands and Wildlands. The use of HYDE 3.2 data inputs, and the goal of including Earth’s entire terrestrial surface in the maps, not just ice-free land, required slight adjustments to the rule-based classification of Anthromes 2.0, leading to an updated classification algorithm and classification legend: the Anthromes 2.1 classification. The HYDE 3.2 “grazing” area variable was used in the same way as the original, “pasture” variable of HYDE 3.1, to which it is equivalent. In contrast with the 19 original anthrome classes covering Earth’s ice-free land in the Anthromes 2.0 classification. Anthromes 2.1 covers all of Earth’s land surface with 20 anthrome classes, by including an anthrome class for uninhabited ice-covered land areas. Taken together, HYDE 3.2 now provides all data needed to compute anthromes classes without reference to other global map layers, therefore avoiding potential artifacts and errors introduced by differences across datasets in land/sea masks, classification definitions and spatial resolutions. Differences between anthrome maps caused by the change in input data from HYDE 3.1 plus additional data inputs, to the use of HYDE 3.2 exclusively, were assessed by comparing maps directly using statistical measures of association, by comparing land area tabulations for anthrome classes in comparable time periods, and by comparing maps using a GIS to highlight differences in data inputs and anthrome classification across the planet. Land areas were computed for Anthromes 2.0 classes using the original land area data layer for this dataset and for Anthromes 12K using the HYDE 3.2 land area data layer. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2073-445X/9/5/129) ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The source shows information for over 73 time steps from 10,000 BC to 2015 AD; as well as a [Discrete Global Grid version](https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi:10.7910/DVN/E3H3AK) of the dataset. title: Global Hunger Index
description: ### Overview The Global Hunger Index (GHI) is a tool designed to comprehensively measure and track hunger at global, regional, and national levels. GHI scores are calculated each year to assess progress and setbacks in combating hunger. The GHI is designed to raise awareness and understanding of the struggle against hunger, provide a way to compare levels of hunger between countries and regions, and call attention to those areas of the world where hunger levels are highest and where the need for additional efforts to eliminate hunger is greatest. The GHI uses the most up-to-date data available for each of the GHI indicators, meaning the scores are only as current as the data. For the calculation of the 2021 GHI scores, undernourishment data are from 2018–2020; child stunting and child wasting data are from 2016–2020, with the most current data from that range used for each country; and child mortality data are from 2019. In 2021, owing to the COVID-19 pandemic, the values of some of the GHI component indicators, and in turn the GHI scores, are likely to worsen, but any changes that occur in 2021 are not yet reflected in the data and scores in this year’s report. ### Methodology GHI scores are calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger. First, for each country, values are determined for four indicators: 1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient); 2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition); 3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and 4. Child mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments). Second, each of the four component indicators is given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades. Third, standardized scores are aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply; child mortality; and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight (the formula for calculating GHI scores is provided in [Appendix B](https://www.globalhungerindex.org/pdf/en/2021/appendix-b.pdf)). Data used in the calculation of GHI scores come from various UN and other multilateral agencies. The GHI scores presented here reflect the latest revised data available for the four indicators. title: Fires
description: ### Overview This dataset includes near-real-time active fires as points that represent the center of a 375 m resolution pixel and is being updated twice daily. The data is collected from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) sensor on Suomi-National Polar-Orbiting Partnership (Suomi-NPP) satellite. This dataset is provided through the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) Fire Email Alerts. This dataset provides improved response for smaller fires, mapping of large fire perimeters, and better detection at night, when fire activities usually occur. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of detection. This dataset is well suited for use in near-real time alert systems, fire tracking, and management. ### Methodology Fire detections are determined using a multispectral contextual algorithm to identify subpixel fire activity and other thermal anomalies in the Level 1 (swath) input data. The algorithm uses all five 375 m VIIRS channels to detect fires and separate land, water, and cloud pixels in the image. Fire locations are then given as the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The algorithm first screens for cloud and water pixels. Next potential fires are found using criteria based on brightness detected by the channels. These fires are then filtered by the algorithm to find the distinct radiometric signatures associated with active fires. Finally custom filters are applied to reduce false alarm rates. False alarms usually come from areas of high solar reflection such as metallic rooftops in industrial parks or bright surfaces such as concrete pavement. Confidence values are available for each fire detection. They are based on a collection of intermediate algorithm quantities used in the detection process and are intended to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot/fire pixels. Confidence values are set to low, nominal, and high. Low confidence daytime fire pixels are typically associated with areas of sun glint and lower relative temperature anomaly (<15K) in the mid-infrared channel I4. Nominal confidence pixels are those free of potential sun glint contamination during the day and marked by strong (>15K) temperature anomaly in either day or nighttime data. High confidence fire pixels are associated with day or nighttime saturated pixels. For the full documentation of the initial algorithm methodology, please see the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425713004483). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Resource Watch displays the most recent fires in the past week. Data older than the last seven days or within the temporal coverage of January 20, 2012, to the present is available from the data provider. Satellite-Detected Vegetation Health
description: MODIS NDVI data are provided by NASA through its Terra and Aqua satellites and made available through the Global Agricultural Monitoring (GLAM) project. Data are released in 8-day periods, with January 1 always being the starting date of the first period of each year. The data are released on a 0.00225 x 0.00225 degree grid, resulting in ~250-meter square sections that cover the entire globe. This data can be, and are operationally, used to classify land cover on the Earth's surface. This classification can be used to monitor crop health and forest cover around the world through programs like USAID's FEWS NET and WRI's Global Forest Watch (GFW). The Terra and Aqua satellites each carry a MODIS instrument, image the same areas on the Earth approximately 3 hours apart, and return to each point on Earth every 1-2 days. The data shown here are for the Terra satellite only. The Terra MODIS sensors collect data on several spectral bands, one of which corresponds to the reflectance of visible red spectrum of light (Band 1, 620-670 nm, VIS) and one of which corresponds to the reflectance near infrared spectrum of light (Band 2, 841-876 nm, NIR). The NDVI is calculated based on differences in reflectance of these bands of light off the Earth's surface. NDVI = (NIR - VIS) / (NIR + VIS). For additional information, please see https://glam1.gsfc.nasa.gov, https://nsidc.org/data/modis/terra_aqua_differences/, and https://arset.gsfc.nasa.gov/land/webinars/advancedNDVI. title: Uttarakhand Wheat Projections
description: The data displays model-based projections for wheat yield for the baseline (1981-2010) and mid-century (2021-2050) periods under RCP 4.5 & 8.5 (in Tons/ha). This data is an output from the DSSAT (Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer) model which simulates growth, development and yield of a crop growing on a uniform area of land under prescribed or simulated management as well as the changes in soil water, carbon, and nitrogen that take place under the cropping system over time. The main factors affecting crop yield include air temperature, relative humidity, solar radiation, wind speed, water availability, and atmospheric CO2 concentration. Increase in temperature adversely affects crop physiology and results in decreasing crop yields and grain quality. Increase in atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide may lead to increase plant growth of certain crops. DSSAT can be used at a farm level to determine the impact of climate change on crop production and potential adaptation practices that should be developed for farmers. DSSAT outputs can be used in economic models which are designed to estimate the potential impacts of climate change on production, consumption, income, gross domestic product (GDP), employment, and farm value. title: Clean Energy Investment Potential
description: ### Overview This dataset includes a comprehensive index for clean energy sector investment in 104 developing nations. These nations include 100 countries that are classified as less developed according to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), along with Chile, Mexico, Turkey, and Qatar, which are important developing nations with emerging clean energy markets. This index, formally known as the Climatescope index, is crucial in showing clean energy investment potential amid rapidly changing market circumstances. This [Climatescope](http://global-climatescope.org/) index is developed by BloombergNEF and supported by the UK Department for International Development. This tool is intended for use by investors, companies, governments, nongovernmental organizations (NGOs), researchers, communities, and others seeking to evaluate the opportunities of investing in clean energy. ### Methodology The scores were calculated based on three topics with their associated weights in parentheses: fundamentals (50%), opportunities (25%), and experience (25%). A total of 167 different indicators and subindicators were used to score these topics. Each of the three topics is described below: - **Fundamentals** assessed the fundamental structures that encourage clean energy to prosper. Indicators for *Fundamentals* described a country’s clean energy policies, power sector structure, regulations, and local barriers to renewable energy development. Example indicators included domestic climate change laws, nationally determined contribution (NDC) target coverage, and climate change mitigation incentives. - **Opportunities** analyzed future opportunities for clean energy growth in a country. Indicators for *Opportunities* represented a country’s current and future electricity demand, its energy consumption, carbon dioxide emissions from the power sector, and short- and medium-term opportunities for renewable energy procurement. Example indicators included electrification rate, the growth rate of generation, and upcoming renewable auctions. - **Experience** reflected the track record to host clean energy development successfully in a country. Indicators for *Experience* described a country’s historical levels of renewable energy investment, the comprehensiveness of its nonmanufacturing clean energy value chain, and the volume of installed clean energy. The assumption was that markets with greater experience deploying renewable energy usually offer lower risks for investors. Example indicators included the capacity of clean energy that has been installed, foreign investment in renewables, and the number of clean energy service providers. To collect data, BloombergNEF analysts made 23 countries visits to conduct interviews, in addition to desktop research. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://global-climatescope.org/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Flood Risk
description: The Aqueduct Global Flood Risk Maps measures river flood impacts by urban damage, affected GDP, and affected population at the country, state, and river basin scale across the globe, as well as 120 cities. The maps estimate current flood risk for a specific geographic unit, taking into account existing local flood protection levels. They project future flood risk with three climate and socio-economic change scenarios. For the current scenario, hydrological data from 1960 through 1999 were used for generating flood inundations for 9 return periods, from 2-year flood to 1000-year flood, and 2010 GDP, population, and land use data for assessing flood impacts. For future projections, the following scenarios were used: 5 GCMs (Global Climate Models) from CMIP5 (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5) projecting future flood inundations under two climate scenarios, RCP4.5 (Representative Concentration Pathway) and RCP8.5, and projected socio-economic changes using SSP2 (Shared Socio-economic Pathway) and SSP3, from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Assessment Report 5. title: Projected Permafrost Loss
description: Projected permafrost extents, created through the research of Chadburn et al. (2017), estimates a sensitivity of permafrost area loss to global mean warming at stabilization of 2°C. The latest climate models all predict warming of high-latitude soils and thus thawing of permafrost under future climate change, but with widely varying magnitudes of permafrost thaw. It is estimated that permafrost area will eventually be reduced by over 40% if the climate is stabilized at 2°C above preindustrial levels. This research showed that it is possible to infer the sensitivity of permafrost to future global warming by using present-day spatial distribution of permafrost and mean annual air temperature (MAAT). Permafrost extent is estimated at a 0.5 degree spatial resolution and is restricted to the Northern Hemisphere. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. Tree Cover Loss
description: This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis & Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, USGS, and NASA, measures areas of tree cover loss across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at approximately 30 × 30 meter resolution. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 5 thematic mapper (TM), the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+), and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) sensors. Over 1 million satellite images were processed and analyzed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval, and more than 400,000 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 images for updates for the 2011-2017 interval. The clear land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled and a supervised learning algorithm was applied to identify per pixel tree cover loss. In this data set, “tree cover” is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters in height, and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Tree cover loss is defined as “stand replacement disturbance,” or the complete removal of tree cover canopy at the Landsat pixel scale. Tree cover loss may be the result of human activities, including forestry practices such as timber harvesting or deforestation (the conversion of natural forest to other land uses), as well as natural causes such as disease or storm damage. Fire is another widespread cause of tree cover loss, and can be either natural or human-induced. This data set has been updated five times since its creation, and now includes loss up to 2017 (Version 1.5). The analysis method has been modified in numerous ways, including new data for the target year, re-processed data for previous years (2011 and 2012 for the Version 1.1 update, 2012 and 2013 for the Version 1.2 update, and 2014 for the Version 1.3 update), and improved modelling and calibration. These modifications improve change detection for 2011-2017, including better detection of boreal loss due to fire, smallholder rotation agriculture in tropical forests, selective losing, and short cycle plantations. Eventually, a future “Version 2.0” will include reprocessing for 2000-2010 data, but in the meantime integrated use of the original data and Version 1.5 should be performed with caution. title: Fire Weather
description: The Fire Weather data set is derived from the Fire Weather Index (FWI) System, which was developed by the Canadian Forest Service and is the most widely used fire danger rating system in the world. The Global Fire WEather Database (GFWED) is a global database of daily FWI System calculations, produced by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Institute for Space Studies. This system combines different weather factors that may influence the start and spread of a vegetation fire and is comprised of three moisture codes and three fire behavior indices. The moisture codes describe the moisture content of three general fuel classes. The fire behavior indices describe the rate of spread, fuel consumption and intensity of a fire if it were to start. The data inputs for these calculations are measurements of 12:00 local time temperature at 2 m, relative humidity at 2 m and wind speed at 10 m. Daily snow-depth and precipitation were totaled over the previous 24 hours. GFWED includes several different versions of these calculations, each of which uses a different input weather and precipitation data. The version of these calculations shown on Resource Watch uses input data from GEOS-5 for temperature, relative humidity, wind-speed and snow depth; input precipitation comes from the 'Late' version of GPM IMERG Daily Precipitation. Global daily calculations of the FWI System indices using these data inputs are available from 2015 to present with 0.1° resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set.
