Understanding active volcanoes, their trends, and how to predict them serves as a way of protecting people and understanding how the Earth was formed. description: The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in the average number of days of extreme heat at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme heat day is a day where the maximum temperature is greater than the 99th percentile maximum temperature during the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. Temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, an increased quantity of extreme heat days can lead to human and ecosystem threats caused by more frequent, more intense, and longer heat waves. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference. The average number of extreme heat days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily maximum temperature values for a given year and summing the number of days where the maximum temperature was greater than the 99th percentile temperature during the baseline period. The number of extreme heat days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in extreme heat days. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Human Impacts on Oceans
description: The Human Impacts on Oceans data set identifies the areas of the oceans that are most- and least- impacted by human stressors. This 5 km resolution global map was created by Stanford University (Stanford), Imperial College London (Imperial), and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB). This study considered 20 ocean ecosystem types and 19 stressors. The 19 stressors considered were artisanal fishing, 5 types of commercial fishing (pelagic vs. demersal, high vs. lowbycatch, destructive of habitat vs. nondestructive), commercial shipping, inorganic pollution, organic pollution, nutrient pollution, ocean-based pollution, light pollution, invasive species, 4 climate-change stressors (warming, acidification, sea-level rise, UV changes), direct human use, and oil rigs. Stressor inputs into the model come from data sets for years ranging from 1981 to 2013. The sensitivity of each ecosystem type to each stressor was determined by surveying 135 experts from 19 countries, and these sensitivities were used to weight the impacts of the stressors in different areas of the ocean. Modeling the vulnerability of ecosystems is challenging for many reasons. Ecosystem response to different stressors is often simplified for model development and the combined effects of multiple stressors on an ecosystem are not always well-understood. Additionally, relevant data may be missing or contain errors. Ignoring this uncertainty can lead to poor ocean management decisions. This map identifies regions of the oceans with high and low human impacts that were robust to these uncertainties, meaning that these areas were identified as being highly or minimally impacted by humans in simulations run over a range of plausible ecological conditions. Seven different factors of uncertainty were tested in 3000 simulations, each of which produced a map of the human impact on different parts of the ocean. Within each map, the 25% of ocean areas with the highest and lowest human impacts, respectively, were identified. The number of times each grid cell was categorized as a high-impact area or a low-impact area was counted. This map shows grid cells that were identified in each category in 75-90% of the simulation runs (High/Low Impact Likely) and in over 90% of the simulation runs (High/Low Impact Very Likely). Mangrove Extent Change
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the change in the global extent of mangroves between 1996 and 2016. Comparable maps of mangrove gain and loss (corresponding to smaller timesteps) were part of the creation of the first global map of mangrove extent produced via an automated, reproducible, and globally consistent methodology, which used a combination of optical and radar satellite data. The data have an effective resolution of approximately 25 meters at the equator. Mangroves are forested intertidal ecosystems that perform critical landscape-level functions related to the regulation of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment inputs into marine areas. They play a key role in helping to control the quality of marine coastal waters. Mangroves are of critical importance as breeding and nursery sites for birds, fish, and crustaceans. Additionally, they constitute important sinks for carbon storage. Once abundant along the world’s tropical and subtropical coastlines, mangroves are in global decline. Significant drivers of change include removal for aquaculture, agriculture, energy exploitation and other industrial development, with an unknown proportion of the remaining mangroves fragmented and degraded. Mangroves are also sensitive to climate change effects such as sea level rise, temperature extremes, and changes in hydrology. The underlying mangrove extent dataset has been generated by the [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) – a collaboration between Aberystwyth University (U.K.), solo Earth Observation (soloEO), Wetlands International, the World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). DOB Ecology supported the mapping in Africa through the Mangrove Capital Africa project. ### Methodology The net extent change in global mangrove area from 1996 to 2016 was calculated by comparing the [global mangrove extent maps](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/45) provided by [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) for the corresponding years. **1996 and 2016 extent maps:** To develop the 1996 and 2016 mangrove extent maps, GMW first created a baseline map of mangroves for 2010 at a global level through a random forests classification of both Landsat sensor spectral composite data (all spectral wavebands) and Advanced Land Observing Satellite (ALOS) Phased Arrayed L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data.The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was generated based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on randomly sampling 38 million points using historical mangrove maps (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017). The maps for 1996 and 2016 were derived by detection and classification of losses (defined as a decrease in radar backscatter) and gains (defined as a backscatter increase) between the 2010 ALOS PALSAR data and JERS-1 SAR (1996) and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 (2016) data. The change pixels for each year in question were then added or removed from the 2010 baseline raster mask (buffered to allow detection of mangrove gains also immediately outside of the mask) to produce the new extent maps. Classification accuracies of the changes were assessed with over 45,000 points, with an overall accuracy of 75.0%. **1996–2016 mangrove extent change map:** WRI derived the 1996 to 2016 extent change map by directly comparing the corresponding extent layers provided by GMW (rather than combining the change layers calculated by the authors). This comparison was performed by calculating the geometric intersection of the 1996 and 2016 extent layers. The intersection was erased from the 1996 extent to obtain loss polygons and erased from the 2016 extent to obtain gain polygons. For the full documentation for the 1996 and 2016 extent maps, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/10/10/1669). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows the [mangrove extent time series](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/386314c4-ab42-47a7-b2cd-596b788e114d), which shows total mangrove forest cover, rather than change. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [GitHub](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/for_005a_mangrove). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. Reservoirs and Dams
description: ### Overview This dataset shows the locations of dams and the areas covered by the reservoirs that they create upstream. The information used to create this dataset is compiled from a variety of sources, creating a global, harmonized account of dams and reservoirs. The current version maps 7,320 dams that were built as recently as 2017, with a combined storage capacity of 6,864 km³. These include reservoirs with a storage capacity of more than 0.1 km³; smaller dams and reservoirs were added if data was available. The production of this dataset was led by a consortium of partners through the Global Water System Project (GWSP) in Bonn, Germany, and is a joint project of the Earth System Science Partnership (ESSP). ### Methodology Datasets were contributed by 11 participating institutions to serve as the foundation for creating the first version of this dataset. The current version of the dataset adds new dams and reservoirs that were mostly derived from data sources available online. These included national repositories, the Clean Development Mechanism project registry of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), some privately maintained databases like Roller Compacted Concrete Dams, and, for validation purposes, information listed by the International Commission on Large Dams (ICOLD). To consolidate the datasets and improve accuracy, the locations of all dams included in the source datasets were verified, updated, and/or newly georeferenced. This process was guided by maps, atlases, and online resources (including Google Earth). Each dam (with a few exceptions, see source [methodology](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/100125)) was assigned to a polygon that depicts the reservoir surface. In the first version of the dataset, most polygons used for this procedure were provided by the SRTM Water Body Database (SWBD), a near-global, public mapping product created at 30 m resolution from remote sensing imagery. Additional reservoir outlines were added from various alternative sources or digitized from scratch. In the newest version of the dataset, most of the new reservoir polygons that were added were delineated from the surface water maps produced by the Joint Research Center (JRC) of the European Commission from Landsat imagery at 30 m resolution for the period 1984-2015. Cross-validation of the information provided by different sources was performed, and records with suspicious information were flagged and individually verified. Data gaps were filled by comparing and merging attributes from different databases. If inconsistencies, uncertainties, or data gaps remained, the “Quality” index of the record was lowered accordingly. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1890/100125). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: The Palm Mill locations data come from FoodReg’s Known Sources palm oil mill database and directly from palm oil traders and buyers. The data represent the mills within the supply chain of at least 3 major palm oil buyers who wish to remain anonymous. The data do not represent the entire universe of mills and are only representative of the mills within the supply chains of companies submitting mill data to WRI or Known Sources. The location of mills was self-reported by mill owners. All mill locations were manually verified by WRI using Google Earth imagery according to criteria for mill infrastructure, including the presence of buildings, settling ponds, and nearby palm oil plantations. Mills may have duplicate names when site-level name data are missing and group name information is included. The data will be updated as new data become available to WRI or Known Sources. title: Frost Free Season
description: Frost free season represents the annual average longest streak of days above freezing, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Water Institutions
description: The FAO AQUASTAT Water Institutions database describes approximately 1,000 main institutions within 117 countries dealing with water resources for agriculture and rural development. Information is gathered in each country during the country update processes. The existing list of institutions is then provided with the request to add institutions that have come into existence since the last update, to delete institutions that don't exist anymore (and, if applicable, to replace them with their successors), and/or to add missing information for existing institutions. All institutions are recorded in the institution database. The names of these institutions are listed, along with their type (government, university, etc.), sector (agriculture, irrigation, water, environment, natural resources, etc.), and activities (policy and strategy, infrastructure development, research, etc.). Updates are continuous, whenever new data become available, but mainly during the country update, which takes place once every 5 years at the most. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Aqueduct Seasonal Variability
description: ### Overview Seasonal variability measures the average within-year variability of available water supply, including both renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Higher values indicate wider variations of available supply within a year. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low variability (coefficient of variation <0.33) to extremely high variability (coefficient of variation >1.33). Seasonal variability values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). ### Methodology Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB 2), to calculate five indicators. Seasonal variability is one of those indicators and was calculated using the available water supply time series from the default PCR-GLOBWB 2. Seasonal or within-year variability is defined as the coefficient of variation (CV) of available water between months in a year for each sub-basin. The CV was calculated by dividing the standard deviation (SD) of the available water supply within a year by the year’s mean available water supply. Finally, raw baseline seasonal variability were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw seasonal variability values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds. - Low (0-1): < 0.33 - Low to medium (1-2): 0.33 - 0.66 - Medium to high (2-3): 0.66 - 1.0 - High (3-4): 1.0 - 1.33 - Extremely high (4-5): > 1.33 For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Tree Cover Loss
description: This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis & Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, USGS, and NASA, measures areas of tree cover loss across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at approximately 30 × 30 meter resolution. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 5 thematic mapper (TM), the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+), and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) sensors. Over 1 million satellite images were processed and analyzed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval, and more than 400,000 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 images for updates for the 2011-2017 interval. The clear land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled and a supervised learning algorithm was applied to identify per pixel tree cover loss. In this data set, “tree cover” is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters in height, and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Tree cover loss is defined as “stand replacement disturbance,” or the complete removal of tree cover canopy at the Landsat pixel scale. Tree cover loss may be the result of human activities, including forestry practices such as timber harvesting or deforestation (the conversion of natural forest to other land uses), as well as natural causes such as disease or storm damage. Fire is another widespread cause of tree cover loss, and can be either natural or human-induced. This data set has been updated five times since its creation, and now includes loss up to 2017 (Version 1.5). The analysis method has been modified in numerous ways, including new data for the target year, re-processed data for previous years (2011 and 2012 for the Version 1.1 update, 2012 and 2013 for the Version 1.2 update, and 2014 for the Version 1.3 update), and improved modelling and calibration. These modifications improve change detection for 2011-2017, including better detection of boreal loss due to fire, smallholder rotation agriculture in tropical forests, selective losing, and short cycle plantations. Eventually, a future “Version 2.0” will include reprocessing for 2000-2010 data, but in the meantime integrated use of the original data and Version 1.5 should be performed with caution. title: Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Forecasts
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Forecasts dataset provides air quality forecasts for a group of cities taking part in the [CityAQ project](https://airquality.gsfc.nasa.gov/cityaq-pilot-combine-local-monitoring-data-geos-cf-model-outputs-develop-city-scale-operational). Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations are forecasted at the station level, and are shown in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). The dataset is updated daily and shows the forecasted concentration of PM2.5 for the following five days. The forecast is generated by the source at an hourly time step, and Resource Watch aggregates to a 24-hour average. PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/particulate-matter-pm-basics) the size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even go into the bloodstream. The CityAQ project aims to help cities around the world to know more about the levels, sources, and impacts of air pollution. Many of the places with the highest level of pollution have the least information to work with to know their air quality and manage it accordingly. Free and publicly-available air quality data from satellites, along with low-cost sensor systems and output from air quality models, have the potential to augment high-quality, regulatory-grade data in countries with in situ monitoring networks and provide much needed air quality information in countries without them. By combining the strengths of these multiple monitoring technologies, an integrated air pollution network has the potential to provide free/low cost and publicly-accessible air quality information to health and air quality managers in cities around the world. These forecasts were modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) by combining local air quality monitoring information, made available with support from the World Resources Institute (WRI), with the outputs of NASA’s global Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). The CityAQ project objective is to provide participating cities with useful forecasts that they can use to anticipate air quality events, communicate with stakeholders, and manage local interventions more effectively. It looks to test and refine a methodology for combining locally held information with globally consistent analysis to offer new local tools and, in the future, potentially improve global analysis by aggregating fragmented local data into programmatically useful datasets and make the GEOS-CF forecasts usable by all world cities. The organizations involved in the CityAQ project aim to refine a scalable approach for engaging with users to co-create air quality tools that leverage and extend existing scientific analysis. ### Methodology Validated or raw station level measurement data is collected from either government sites or [OpenAQ](https://openaq.org/#/). Validated air quality observations of government sites were obtained from the air quality data portals of [Bogotá](http://rmcab.ambientebogota.gov.co/home/map) and [Sao Paulo](https://servicos.cetesb.sp.gov.br/qa/), or in the case of the Mexican cities of Monterrey, Guadalajara, Salamanca and León were shared directly by state governments. Near-real time, raw observations for the cities of Addis, Jakarta, as well as the following cities in the mexican state of Guanajuato: Guanajuato city, Irapuato, San Miguel de Allende, Silao, Celaya, San Luis de la Paz and Abasolo were retrieved from OpenAQ. For station-level data to be included in OpenAQ’s catalogue, it must meet the minimum data requirements as described by [OpenAQ](https://github.com/openaq/openaq-fetch/blob/master/README.md). Meteorological and atmospheric chemistry information at each of the CityAQ stations is obtained from NASA’s GEOS-CF model. GEOS-CF provides global hourly analyses and forecasts of atmospheric composition at 25-kilometer spatial resolution. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. Any correlation between cloud cover and surface PM2.5 should be captured similarly by GCC and GOCART. The PM2.5 dataset shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GCC module. A detailed description of GEOS-CF can be found in [Keller et al. (2021)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1029/2020MS002413). Since the model output is too coarse to resolve fine-scale air quality features characteristic of urban environments, a bias-correction algorithm is applied to account for the spatial representation error, as well as other potential model biases such as errors in the model representation of transport or chemistry. The bias-correction methodology uses the [XGBoost machine learning algorithm](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#) to develop a machine learning model that predicts the model bias at each of the observation stations as a function of the current meteorological and chemical environment and time. Once trained, the machine learning model is used on a daily basis to calculate the expected model bias at a given site and this value is added to the ‘raw’ (i.e., uncorrected) GEOS-CF predictions. The machine learning training is based on the 2018–2019 observation–model differences and designed to predict the systematic model bias between hourly PM2.5 observations and the model predictions at that location. These biases can be due to errors in the model, such as emission estimates, sub-grid-scale local influences or meteorology and chemistry. Since model biases are often site-specific, a separate machine learning model is used for each site. The input features to the machine learning algorithm encompass 9 meteorological parameters (as simulated by the GEOS-CF model: surface northward and eastward wind components, surface temperature and skin temperature, surface relative humidity, total cloud coverage, total precipitation, surface pressure, and planetary boundary layer height) and the modeled surface concentrations of 51 chemical species (O3, NOx, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and aerosols). In addition, it provides as input features the hour-of-day, day of week, and month of the year; these allow the machine learning model to identify systematic observation-model mismatches related to the diurnal, weekly and seasonal cycle of the pollutants. This bias correction methodology is based on [Keller et al. (2021)](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/21/3555/2021/). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows CityAQ datasets for [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/403726e5-6852-49f4-9dce-b82b599b09fc) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/8ee6a93b-ab7a-41a8-95f5-3d684626d9ea). title: Projected Change in Frost Free Season (RCP4.5)
description: The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

description: OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. title: Air Quality: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Satellite Measurements
description: ### Overview The Air Quality: CO Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of carbon monoxide (CO) densities in the total atmospheric column. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of CO found between Earth’s surface and the top of the atmosphere. The CO density is reported with units of moles of CO per square meter of air (mol/m²). Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas that can be harmful when inhaled in large amounts. CO is released during combustion, so the largest outdoor sources of CO are cars, trucks and other vehicles, and machinery that burn fossil fuels. Breathing air with a high concentration of CO reduces the amount of oxygen that can be transported in the bloodstream to critical organs like the heart and brain. At very high levels, which are possible indoors or in other enclosed environments, CO can cause dizziness, confusion, unconsciousness, and death. Very high levels of CO are not likely to occur outdoors. However, when CO levels are elevated outdoors it can be of particular concern to people with preexisting heart disease. These people already have a reduced ability for getting oxygenated blood to their heart. They are especially vulnerable to the effects of CO when exercising or under increased stress. In these situations, short-term exposure to elevated CO may result in reduced oxygen to the heart accompanied by chest pain also known as angina. The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as CO, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution. Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). ### Methodology The TROPOMI CO dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. CO data was collected by determining the amount of sunlight reflected by the troposphere in the 2.3 µm spectral range of the solar spectrum. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that CO molecules produce in the atmosphere. The CO data collected using this method was then input into the Shortwave Infrared CO Re- trieval (SICOR) algorithm created by the Netherlands Institute for Space Research. Along with CO data, the following information was input into SICOR: - Relative profile of CO and water in the atmosphere for a given region - Solar/viewing geometry and geo-location of the S5P satellite - Temperature, water vapor/pressure profiles, and geo-potential height of the S5P satellite - Estimate of methane (CH₄) abundance as calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model CH₄ estimates were required as CH₄ is used to help filter out the presence of clouds in the model. The algorithm further takes into consideration cloud cover by changing the column sensitivity (altering the minimal amount of light reflection within the column required to determine CO density) according to the light path created by cloud cover. The final results produced by the algorithm were tropospheric vertical column density of CO and the average CO density for the entire vertical column. The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Carbon Monoxide (CO) Total Column”. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO), [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. title: Gini Index
description: ### Overview The Gini index measures economic inequality in a country. Specifically, it is the extent to which the distribution of income (or, in some cases, consumption expenditure) deviates from a perfectly equal distribution among individuals or households within an economy. A Gini index of 0 represents perfect equality, while an index of 100 implies perfect inequality. The Gini index dataset was released by the World Bank. This data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available for the years 1967-present, though most countries only have data for a subset of these years. ### Methodology The Gini Index was calculated from the World Bank’s internationally comparable poverty monitoring database, which draws on income or detailed consumption data from more than 1,000 household surveys across 138 countries in 6 regions and 21 other high-income countries (industrialized economies). To calculate the Gini index, a Lorenz curve plots the cumulative percentages of total income received against the cumulative number of recipients, starting with the poorest individual or household. The Gini index measures the area between the Lorenz curve and a hypothetical (45-degree) line of absolute equality, expressed as a percentage of the maximum area under the line. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SI.POV.GINI/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Agro-Ecological Zones
description: ### Overview The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 (GAEZ v4) dataset assesses current and future agricultural resources and their potential. It is a standardized framework allowing for the characterization of climate, soil, and terrain conditions that are relevant for agricultural production. Data from the First Theme, Land and Water Resources, is displayed here and allows for the uniform classification of [biophysical](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/biophysics) resources that are relevant for agricultural production systems. Outputs are presented at 5 arc minutes resolution, which is approximately 9 km x 9 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. ​​Information on the current and future use of land resources is important for agricultural decision-making with implications on food security, sustainability of land and water resources, and agricultural development and policies. The GAEZ v4 dataset brings together multiple data sources to provide information on the biophysical limitations of land, current crop suitability, and information on how different agricultural resources may be impacted by climate change. Understanding what changes may occur in the future will enable different actors the ability to increase resilience, develop techniques or policies to alleviate potential challenges, and maintain food security. The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) together with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) began developing the GAEZ modeling framework in the early 1980s to provide current data on the state of agricultural resources. It has since expanded to support sustainable agricultural development and provide key information on current and future risks to agricultural production, crop development, land productivity, and impacts from climate change. ### Methodology Multiple datasets were used as inputs to the GAEZ v4 modeling framework and provide data on historic and future climate attributes, soil and terrain resources, land cover, protected land, biodiversity areas, water resources, administrative units, population, and livestock. Historical climate data comes from the Climatic Research Unit TS v3.21 datasets which include monthly climate information. Future climate data for AEZ is derived from climate model outputs for four (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from the fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Data processing was broken into several steps and seven main modules summarize the necessary steps within the GAEZ v4 modeling framework. Outputs from each of the modules are categorized into six main themes: 1) Land and Water Resources, 2) Agro-climatic Resources, 3) Agro-climatic Potential Yield, 4) Suitability and Attainable Yield, 5) Actual Yields and Production, and 6) Yield and Production Gaps. The Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) sub-theme outputs fall under the first Theme, Land and Water Resources, and provides an inventory of land resources for the assessment of land productivity under specific agro-ecological conditions. Thermal and moisture layers are combined with broad categories of soil and terrain qualities allowing for the identification of land areas with biophysical constraints. A rigorous methodology and set of explicit principles are followed to assemble the AEZ classes and definitions. The following principles ensure that: 1) the map classes align with major climate zones based on the baseline historical period of 1981-2010, 2) map classes reflect broad ranges of the length of growing period boundaries, and 3) AEZ classes have generalized information about the prevailing soil and terrain limitations that are derived from GAEZ v4 terrain and soil resources inventories. The final AEZ layer has 57 different classes that are mapped at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 Agro-Ecological Zones data has additional data for 2071-2100 and additional RCPs (2.6 and 6). For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. title: Average Temperature
description: Annual average temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](f05fde43-ce5a-4910-83b1-85dafd39bfbb) as a replacement.**_ The Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect represents the relatively higher temperatures found in urban areas compared to surrounding rural areas owing to higher proportions of impervious surfaces and the release of waste heat from vehicles and heating and cooling systems. Paved surfaces and built structures tend to absorb shortwave radiation from the sun and release long-wave radiation after a lag of a few hours. The Global Urban Heat Island Data Set, 2013, estimates the land surface temperature in urban areas in degrees Celsius (average summer daytime maximum and average summer nighttime minimum) as well as the difference between those temperatures and the temperatures in surrounding rural areas, defined as a 10 km buffer around the urban extent. Urban extents are from SEDAC’s Global Rural-Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMPv1), and land surface temperatures are from SEDAC’s Global Summer Land Surface Temperature (LST) Grids, 2013, which are derived from the Aqua Level-3 Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), Version 5, global daytime and nighttime Land Surface Temperature (LST) 8-day composite data (MYD11A2). For most regions, the UHI data set provides the average daytime maximum (1:30 p.m. overpass) and average nighttime minimum (1:30 a.m. overpass) temperatures in urban and rural areas, and the urban-rural temperature differences, derived from LST data representing a 40-day time span during July-August (Julian days 185-224) in the Northern Hemisphere and January-February (Julian days 001-040) in the Southern Hemisphere. title: Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature (RCP8.5)
description: The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average maximum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the maximum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average maximum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The annual average maximum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily maximum temperature data over a given year. The average annual maximum temperatures were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average maximum temperature. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual maximum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

[Archived] Vulnerability to Climate Change Index
description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](4d2d47c1-fed1-4484-83e3-c91c3f6f7315) as a replacement.**_ The University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) produces an annual index of climate change adaptation potential annually from 1995 to 2015. A country's ND-GAIN score is composed of a vulnerability score and a readiness score. Vulnerability and readiness are based on compiled indicators. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. ND-GAIN measures overall vulnerability by considering 6 life-supporting sectors—food, water, health, ecosystem service, human habitat, and infrastructure—and 36 indicators. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. ND-GAIN measures overall readiness by considering 3 components—economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness—and 9 indicators. Each indicator comes from a public data source. title: Environmental Performance Index
description: The Environmental Performance Index (EPI), produced by the Yale Center for Environmental Law and Policy (YCELP) and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CEISIN), scores countries from 0 to 100 according to each country's relative performance on a set of environmental indicators. High scorers exhibit long-standing policies and programs to protect public health, preserve natural resources, and decrease greenhouse gas emissions. The index is built from 32 national-level indicators relevant to environmental issues, grouped into 11 issues, which are themselves divided into 2 overarching themes: (1) ecosystem vitality and (2) environmental health as it applies to human health. Multiple other data sets were employed to provide context before whittling down to those 32. Each country's value for each indicator is scaled between 0 and 100 to reflect the proximity of its performance in that indicator to best and worst performances. The best performance can either be a statistical measure—such as the 95th percentile of the distribution of all countries' scores—or a scientifically determined target, such as the World Health Organization's designation of safe and dangerous amounts of particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5) in the air we breathe. Setting the target for worst performance follows a similar logic. 1st or 5th percentile was often used depending on the distribution of the underlying data. The 32 indicators, each scored between 0 and 100, are then weighted and aggregated to produce the overall EPI score for a country. The weights used to calculate EPI scores reflect a mixture of emphases determined by subjective best judgment, data quality, and analysis of global trends. A "materiality threshold" is used to determine whether an indicator should count toward a given country's score. Landlocked countries, for example, are not rated according to their marine protected areas or the health of their fisheries. When these indicators are removed, the remaining indicators receive proportionally higher weights in calculating the country total EPI. The datasets used to calculate EPI come from trusted third-party sources like international governing bodies, nongovernmental organizations, and academic research centers. title: Bathymetry
description: ### Overview The Bathymetry dataset is composed of the GEBCO_2019 Grid, which shows terrain elevation around the world, for both land and the ocean floor. It provides global coverage on a 15 arc-second grid. The data values refer to elevations at the center of grid cells in meters. The GEBCO_2019 Grid is the latest global bathymetric product released by the General Bathymetric Chart of the Oceans (GEBCO) and has been developed through the Nippon Foundation-GEBCO [Seabed 2030 Project](https://seabed2030.gebco.net/). This is a collaborative project between the Nippon Foundation of Japan and GEBCO. The Seabed 2030 Project aims to bring together all available bathymetric data to produce the definitive map of the world ocean floor and make it available to all. ### Methodology The grid used Version 1 of the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) 15+ data set as a ‘base’. This dataset is a fusion of land topography with measured and estimated seafloor topography. It is largely based on version 11 of SRTM30+, augmented with the gridded bathymetric data sets developed by the four Seabed 2030 Regional Centers. The Regional Centers compiled gridded bathymetric data sets for their areas of responsibility. These regional grids were then provided to the Global Center. For areas outside of the polar regions, these data sets are in the form of 'sparse grids,' meaning only grid cells that contain data were populated. For the polar regions, complete grids were provided due to the complexities of incorporating data held in polar coordinates. The majority of the work, for the non-polar regions, was done using the 'remove-restore' procedure. This is a two stage process of computing the difference between the new data sets created by regional centers and the 'base' grid SRTM15+. The difference between the datasets was gridded and then added back to the existing 'base' grid. The aim was to achieve a smooth transition between the 'new' and 'base' data sets with minimum disturbance of the existing base data set. The polar and Red Sea datasets were supplied in the form of complete grids and were created using feather blending techniques from GlobalMapper software version 11.0. The compilation of the GEBCO_2019 Grid from these regional data grids, with some additional source data sets, was carried out at the Global Center, with the aim of producing a seamless global terrain model. The global grid consists of 86,400 rows and 43,200 columns, giving 3,732,480,000 data points. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the Type Identifier Grid (TID) is available from the data provider. The TID identifies the type of source data that the corresponding grid cells in the GEBCO Grid are based on. title: Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation
description: ### Overview The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data. ### Methodology The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations. CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference. The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Bonn Challenge Restoration Commitment
description: This data set displays current commitments to the Bonn Challenge by country. Established in 2011, the Bonn Challenge calls for bringing 150 million ha of the world’s deforested and degraded land into restoration by 2020, and 350 million ha by 2030. Underlying the Bonn Challenge is the forest landscape restoration (FLR) approach, which aims to restore ecological integrity at the same time as improving human well-being through multifunctional landscapes. The Bonn Challenge is not a new global commitment but rather a practical means of realizing many existing international commitments, including the CBD Aichi Target 15, the UNFCCC REDD+ goal, and the Rio+20 land degradation neutrality goal. It is an implementation vehicle for national priorities such as water and food security and rural development while contributing to the achievement of international climate change, biodiversity, and land degradation commitments. The Global Partnership on Forest Landscape Restoration (GPFLR) oversees the initiative, with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) acting as the secretariat. title: Groundwater Environments and Recharge Rates
description: The German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) partnered with UNESCO's International Hydrological Programme and the International Association of Hydrogeologists to coordinate the World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP). WHYMAP’s goal is to collect, combine and visualize global hydrogeological data to raise awareness of groundwater resources and promote global discussion on water issues. The Groundwater Environments and Recharge Rates Map is a global map of groundwater resources at a scale of 1:25,000,000 and is used to characterize major groundwater environments and recharge rates. The maps used to characterize groundwater environments were selected by evaluating national, regional and continental maps at scales of 1:1,000,000 to 1:15,000,000. Maps at each of these scales were examined to develop continental maps at a scale of 1:10,000,000, which could then be combined into a global map. Differences in each map’s level of detail, philosophy, approach, hydrogeological interpretation and projection had to be considered when combining these maps. These maps were reviewed and redrawn to improve the consistency of methods for each continent. Hydrogeological mapping experts from different parts of the world contributed their regional knowledge to the final revision of these continental maps before they were combined into a final global map. Groundwater recharge rates represent the years 1961-1990. These values are derived from simulations with the global hydrological model WaterGAP, version 2.1f from the University of Frankfurt/Main, Germany. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Future Precipitation Suitability for Coffee Growth
description: ### Overview These maps show the probability that annual precipitation will be within or outside the range necessary for the growth of coffee (Coffea arabica), as calculated by researchers at World Resources Institute using a combination of historical satellite data and climate simulations of future precipitation. Users can choose to see probabilities of insufficient precipitation, excessive precipitation, or precipitation within coffee’s required range. Because they are probabilities, pixel values range from 0 to 1. Probabilities are available for any location on the globe, for every 10 years from 2020 to 2099. Gridded data is available at a spatial resolution of 0.25 arc degrees, which is approximately 25 kilometers (km) x 25 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Like all agricultural crops, coffee can grow only in locations that meet particular climatic requirements. Coffee requires between 750 mm and 4200 mm of precipitation every year ([FAO ECOCROP]( https://gaez.fao.org/pages/ecocrop)). As global climate patterns change, the locations suitable for growing coffee are likely to shift. It is impossible to predict with certainty where coffee will and will not be able to be grown in the coming decades, but we are able to estimate the probability that any location is suitable. In these maps, we focus on suitability related to precipitation, but similar maps can be generated for coffee’s (and other crops’) temperature ranges, humidity ranges, and combinations of these factors. These maps were generated by the AgriAdapt team at World Resources Institute to support growers, processors, buyers, and investors in making long-term, climate-smart decisions about crops and growing locations. ### Methodology The probabilities are calculated as Bayesian posterior probabilities that yearlong precipitation falls within or outside the range 750 mm – 4200 mm. The prior probability is taken from historical rainfall as reported in the [ERA5](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/CKB/ERA5%3A+data+documentation) reanalysis of satellite data. The prior is updated using the [NEX-GDDP](https://esgf.nccs.nasa.gov/esgdoc/NEX-GDDP_Tech_Note_v0.pdf) downscaled simulation ensemble as evidence. NEX-GDDP includes several greenhouse gas emission scenarios. These calculations used the highest-emitting scenario, RCP8.5. The probability rasters have a spatial resolution of 0.25 arc degrees (approximately 25 km at the equator). The full methodology will be published as a WRI Technical Note (Wong and Mackres, forthcoming). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

title: Human Development Index
description: The Human Development Index (HDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, a sufficient education, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The HDI is calculated for 188 countries annually.
